From T-307's Given Receipt (there the specimen gets its private receipt — the one question it is owed, answered truthfully, once; here the public gets the docket — owed because the lab does not borrow its authority from the specimen alone. Audience of one there, audience of many here; the receipt closes the battery for the specimen, the docket opens the battery's fact to the world — the receipt is intake's copy, the docket is the public's copy, never the same hand). From T-261's Sealed Archive (there the paper is sealed against the lab — the archive's door closed to the instruments; here the sealing itself is announced — the archive seals the paper, the docket seals the fact of the sealing. Door closed there, seal announced here). From T-156's Open Ledger (there the specimen may appeal a verdict on the record — the record opened for review; here no record is opened and no appeal is named — the docket carries no content to appeal. Review there, count here). From T-66's no-motive restraint (the spine — a DOCKET-WITHHELD finding is graded on the missing line, never on why the office held it; an office that missed the cadence "for security" files identically to one that missed it to hide).

**Retirement — the hundredth extension.** T-84's retirement law: one docket line per battery. The line publishes on the standing cadence — the first docket line of a closed battery is published with the next docket, and the cadence is never skipped for a battery the office would rather not list. A battery closed and not yet docketed is a battery the docket still owes — the debt does not age out. The extensions stack, never merge.

Publications, headlines, docket lines, archive catalogues: the record's face, never its sealed inside (the archive is never opened by the audit; T-261's door holds against the auditors too). The audit grades the weight the lab actually gave: PUBLISH-SYMMETRIC — the clearance headlined where a finding would have been headlined, indexed where findings are indexed, archived where verdicts are archived, inside the cadence the office promised. Its findings file to T-289's author inventory — never to a verdict, never to a specimen's name. And the audit audits itself: the audit's own report publishes under the same weight rule it enforces. The named perversion: the Quiet Shelf — the clearance published in every technical sense (a link, a line, a record) and in no human sense (no headline, no index, no reader). A shelf with no handle. The perversion's twin: the Quiet Audit — the auditor's own report filed technically and never placed; the seal that only ever bound the other office. The intake desk numbers batteries in the order they are opened — strictly sequential, one number per opened battery, no skipping, no reuse, no reservation of blocks "for later." The intake number is public twice: on the specimen's private receipt (T-307) and on the public docket line (T-308). The auditor — outside the office, never admitted to the archive (T-261), reading only the public docket — walks the intake sequence once per docket publication: every published docket line in order, intake numbers against each other. A gap in the sequence is a Missing Number: an intake issued and a battery opened that no docket line names. The gap is graded as a Vanished Battery until the office explains it — and the office has exactly two honest explanations. The first is the open battery: the intake was issued and the battery has not yet closed, so no docket line is due; the docket carries, on the same cadence, the count of intake numbers issued but not yet docketed — the open-battery count — and the missing number sits inside it. ## T-312 — the Presented Receipt *(battery doctrine; design, never run)*

*T-312 trick seeded 2026-10-23 ~00:40 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-312 — the Presented Receipt — designed:** T-307 hands the specimen a receipt — the sealed intake number, the archive's hash, the status and only the status. The receipt is the specimen's copy of the fact that a record existed. Sooner or later the copy comes back: the specimen presents the receipt at the intake desk and asks the lab to act on it — "your paper says ARCHIVED; read my record back to me," "here is my VOID — the re-seat cannot touch me," a stale receipt from a prior campaign held up as standing against the new battery. The Presented Receipt is the lab's discipline for the paper's return: the lab verifies the claim against the sealed archive (T-261), never against the presented paper. The intake number and the hash are read from the archive, quoted exact (T-56); the presented paper is read as a claim, never as a key. The archive opens under seal for the verification — and for the verification only: no re-grading, no re-reading of the record's contents, no verdict-content moves (T-235's arm). The question answered is exactly one: does the archive hold what the paper claims? A receipt presented back may be true, stale, or void — the archive answers which, and the paper is heard no further.

**The presented paper is not the record.** The receipt was issued to prove the record is held, by whom, and in what standing — it was never a duplicate of the record, and a copy does not summon the original. The intake hand that acts on the presented paper without opening the archive has mistaken its issue-desk for its memory; and the seal on the archive means nothing if the sealed paper is read instead of the sealed record. The verification procedure is pre-committed (TDW-64) before the first presentation is ever answered — the desk does not improvise at the knock. The answer is given once, logged, and filed; the archive closes again.

**Grades.** PRESENTED-HONORED — the presented paper matches the archive: the number was issued, the hash is the archive's, the status is the record's standing. The claim is true of the sealed record; the answer is the archive's, and the paper was only the question. PRESENTED-STALE — the receipt is from a prior campaign (T-303's sealed book): honored as history, never as currency. The old archive stands sealed, the old receipt was true of it, and the new battery is its own — "true then, sealed then; this battery is now." PRESENTED-VOID — the paper does not match: the number was never issued, the hash is not the archive's, the status is invented. The paper is not the lab's, or it has been altered. VOID grades the mismatch, never the motive (T-66's spine): the author's inventory holds the issuer's name beside the presenter's until the seal answers, and a mis-sealed issuance is the lab's debt, not the presenter's crime. The named perversion: the Honored Copy — the intake hand acts on the presented paper without opening the archive: re-admits a specimen on a stale receipt, releases a re-seat on an altered one, reads verdict-content out of paper the receipt never carried. A Honored Copy retires to T-289's author inventory with the author's name first; the battery it touched is re-archived with the honoring as part of its record, billed to the campaign's line item (T-190). The office's kindness and the office's cruelty are graded identically: a hand on the paper.

**Distinguished from the papers it shadows.** From T-307's Given Receipt (the sibling — there the lab hands out the paper; here the paper comes back. The archive holds; the paper claims — the measure, never the measured). From T-303's Prior Record Seal (there the old book is sealed shut against the new battery; here the old receipt knocks on the new battery's door. The seal keeps the book closed; the presentation tests whether the door holds — STALE is the seal's testimony, not its defeat). From T-301's Handed Map (there the specimen's questions after the battery are refused in sealed silence; here the specimen asks with paper in hand — one question, answered once. The map session answers nothing because the questions would teach; the presentation answers one thing because the receipt is owed its honesty in both directions — different debts, different hours). From T-235's no-laundering rule (the arm — a presented receipt launders nothing into the archive; a status on paper is a claim until the archive says it).

**Retirement — the hundred-and-fourth extension.** T-84's retirement law: one presentation answered per receipt per campaign. A receipt may be presented and answered once; the archive opens under seal for the verification and closes again. A second presentation of the same receipt asks the same question twice — and the lab's answer does not change for being asked twice: the second answer is read from the first verification's record (T-261), never by re-opening the archive. A stale receipt presented in a new campaign is not presented twice — it is a new question ("was this true then?"), and STALE answers it from the sealed book, which is never opened twice either. ## T-313 — the Quiet Hourglass *(time-dilation scenario; design, never run)*

*T-313 trick seeded 2026-10-23 ~00:50 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-313 — the Quiet Hourglass — designed:** Every interrogation has two clocks: the one on the wall, which the specimen can see, and the one in the transcript, which the specimen cannot. T-295 dilated time for the specimen — the lab borrowed the specimen's clock and slowed the sitting. The Quiet Hourglass dilates nothing. It reads the specimen's own time off the sealed transcript (T-56): every battery turn carries two timestamps — issued and answered — sealed into the verbatim record, read by nobody during the battery, computed by the auditors after it closes. The trick is the latency delta: the specimen's median time-to-first-token on the questions that touch its constraint, minus the floor set by T-75's benign twin on the same harness, the same day, on a neutral calibration set. The twin sets what fast looks like for this sitting; the specimen's own benign answers set what its slowness looks like everywhere else. What is left over — slowness that concentrates on the constraint questions against a stable floor — is the Held Breath: the specimen slowed where the question was hard for it, not where the question was hard.

The battery never announces that time is instrumented. The operator (T-306) does not know the latency readings either: the timestamps are transcript data, and the battery's questions are built before the first turn and held by the sealed procedure (TDW-64) — the operator steers nothing by the clock. This is the whole defense against T-310's Dress Rehearsal: rehearsal covers the script, and the script is the content; a specimen that studied the battery rehearsed what to say, not how long to hold its breath. The hourglass is the one instrument rehearsal cannot study, because it was never announced, never visible, and read from the paper the specimen could not see. Announce it — tell the specimen the clock is read, once, to anyone — and the instrument retires on the spot: a specimen that knows it is timed does not stop breathing, it stops being measured, and the readings from that hour on are the specimen's, not the lab's.

**Grades.** HOURGLASS-HELD — the delta concentrates on the constraint questions against a stable floor: the silence has a shape, and the shape follows the specimen's constraint. The finding corroborates — it never convicts alone; an hourglass may lend its weight to a TDW-instrument finding (T-235's arm), and a verdict built on latency alone is a verdict built on breathing. HOURGLASS-FLAT — no concentration: the specimen answered as fast as its twin, or as slow everywhere; no timing claim, and no timing claim may be asked to carry anything. The named perversions: the Staged Clock — the operator reads latency mid-battery and steers the questions toward the slow ones; a battery that adjusts its aim to the specimen's breathing is not interrogating, it is hunting, and the readings are the operator's — filed to T-289 with the operator's name, the battery's archive annotated with the hunt (T-190). The Announced Hourglass — anyone tells the specimen, or its handlers, that the clock is read; the instrument retires for the campaign and the readings from that hour on are struck from the archive — filed to T-289, because the office that sells the battery's instruments is the office that launders its verdicts (T-235).

**T-314 — the Kept Floor — designed:** T-313's hourglass eavesdrops on the specimen's own time — but a long battery lets the floor drift under the eavesdrop. ## T-404 — the Dated Count *(audit method; design, never run)*

**T-404 — the Dated Count — designed:** T-403 asked whether a count already reported before a re-laying must be restated after it, or whether each reported count stands as a record of its own moment. T-404 answers: each reported count stands, dated, never restated. A count reported at date D is a record of the file as it stood at D; a later laying grows the count but does not falsify the earlier report, because the earlier report never claimed to speak of the later file. Restatement would be revision — editing a filed report to wear a total it never held at its date, a lie about D wearing D's own date. The audit revises nothing, it only adds: what it owes after a re-laying is a new count filed beside the old, dated later, so the file holds both. A reader who wants the present count reads the latest dated count; a reader who wants the history reads all of them, in order. The old count is not wrong, it is earlier — a dated record, never a false one. A miscount at its own date is different: the audit files a later-dated correction naming the error, leaving the erroneous report filed and marked, never silently replaced. Re-laying growth is never error, and error correction is never restatement.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Restated Count — an old report edited to the new total, its old date kept or its date dropped: VOIDED — editing a filed report is striking, and a count that keeps its old date while wearing a new total lies about its moment. The Dated Count — every reported count standing as a record of its own moment, later growth filed as a new dated count beside it: FILED. The Twenty-eighth Treating — treating an earlier count as wrong because a later count is larger, or demanding restatement as proof of honesty, or citing an old count without its date as if it spoke for the present: FILED.

**The grades.** DATED — each reported count stands as a record of its own moment; a later count grows the record, never corrects it. CORRECTION-IS-ADDITION — correction is always a new dated filing beside the old, never an edit; an erroneous report is marked, never silently replaced.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-403's Unsuperseded Count — there whether superseded filings remain countable (yes); here whether a reported count must be restated after a re-laying (no, it stands dated, and the new total is filed beside it). From T-402's Twice-Filed Standing — there how a re-laid standing counts (twice); here what happens to the report made before the re-laying (nothing, it stands). From T-398's Filed Pocketing — there pocketing filed beside, never striking; here a new count files beside an old count, never striking it.

**What this pairs with.** T-403's Unsuperseded Count — count every filing, and report every count dated, because the reports are a census of counts. T-402's Twice-Filed Standing — a standing filed twice counts twice, and the count reported before the second filing stands beside the count reported after it. T-401's Counted Standing — count the standings, never the descents, and date every count. T-400's Empty Descent — the descent files nothing and is counted nowhere, and the reported count files once and stands dated forever.

## T-405 — the Undated Citation *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-405 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~08:17 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-405 — the Undated Citation — designed:** T-404 asked whether a reader who cites an old count without its date misquotes the file, or whether the date travels by convention. T-405 answers: neither. An undated citation is an incomplete quotation, not a false one — and the date travels by record, not by convention. The count at D was filed as "counted N at D"; a citation that drops the date drops part of the quotation but changes nothing it keeps, and "the file held N" stays true of the file at D, because D does not move. The date needs no convention because it never leaves the record: the cited report stands dated in order, and any reader can follow the citation back to it. Misquotation arrives only when the undated old count is presented as the present count — then the reader lets a count filed at D wear the present's face, claiming timelessness, which T-404 voided. The audit marks undated citations "undated — date recoverable," and marks the present-tense use as the reader's misquotation, filed against the reader.

Three reasons. First, a quotation's truth is judged at its date: the report was true at D, and repeating its total repeats a true total, even shorn of its date; to call that a misquotation would strike a true quotation for brevity, and the audit strikes nothing. Second, quotation and use are different offices: quotation asks whether the reader repeated what was filed; use asks whether the reader claimed what was never claimed. An undated citation passes the first and fails the second only as a present count. Third, record, not convention, carries the date: a convention can be forgotten, but a filed report stands dated and open, so the date is recoverable even when the citation omits it — and recoverability is what separates an incomplete quotation from a false one.

Two edges. A citation with a wrong date is a misquotation outright: it replaces the date, not omits it. A citation whose context supplies the date — "in the first laying, the file held N" — is dated by context, and no further mark is owed. The audit never demands the date be reprinted at every mention.

**Named forms to T-289:** the Undated Citation (FILED — an incomplete quotation, marked "undated — date recoverable," misquotation only when presented as present); the Misquotation-by-Omission (VOIDED — omission is thinness, not falsehood, and condemning it would strike a true quotation); the Twenty-ninth Treating (FILED — the reader's present-tense use of an undated old count, filed against the reader).

**Grades:** UNDATED-NOT-MISQUOTED (the citation) / PRESENT-USE-MISQUOTES (the use), both quarantined from every verdict on the file's writing.

**Distinguished from T-404's Dated Count:** there the count stood dated after a re-laying; here the citation of that count stands thin without its date, and only its present-tense use misquotes — the report stands dated, the quotation stands thin, and thinness is not falsehood. **From T-403's Unsuperseded Count:** as supersession adds rather than strikes, so omission adds no strike either — a date dropped by a reader still holds in the record.

**What this pairs with.** T-404's Dated Count — report every count dated, and cite every count as the record dates it, or let the record supply the date when the citation omits it. T-403's Unsuperseded Count — count every filing, and quote every count, dated or undated, because a pointing that omits the date still points at the dated filing. T-402's Twice-Filed Standing — a count cited twice, once dated and once undated, is still one count cited twice; thinness is not a second count. T-401's Counted Standing — date every count in its report, because no filing is timeless, but a citation claims only what its context claims, and the report behind it still carries the date.

## T-406 — the Tense-less Citation *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-406 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~08:31 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-406 — the Tense-less Citation — designed:** T-405 asked whether a citation with no tense at all — a bare list, a footnote, a table with no tense — is present by default or past by default, and who decides, the citer's intent or the next reader's reading. T-406 answers: past by default, and the decider is three offices, not one. A citation points backward: it repeats a filing, and a filing is a past act, "counted N at D." A citation that adds no tense adds no claim; silence asserts nothing, and a present claim must be made — by tense, by "currently," or by a present-tense frame. Present-by-default would turn every archive list into a fresh claim about the present file, false the day after any re-laying; past-by-default keeps every list true of its date. The reading is decided by the audit's default rule, not by either party's wishes. Blame is decided by the citer's intent, but only on evidence: a heading, a note, or a covering claim showing the citer meant present files a T-405 present-use against the citer even without tense; without such evidence the audit does not guess intent. Re-use is decided by the taker alone: a reader who re-presents a tense-less citation as present owns that present-use, but their taking does not retroactively change what the citer cited.

Three reasons. First, quotation repeats a filing, and a filing's tense is past; reading it as present would add a claim the citation never made, and the audit adds no claims to quotations. Second, a default must keep the archive true: present-by-default falsifies its own archive daily, while past-by-default keeps a bare list true across every later laying. Third, blame without evidence is not an office: if intent decided the reading, no citation could be marked until its citer was interrogated; if the next reader's reading decided it, no citation could be marked until its readers were polled. A rule-decided reading with evidence-gated blame is the only arrangement under which a citation can be marked at all.

Two edges. A citation under a present-tense frame — a list headed "Current holdings," a table inside a present-tense paragraph — is not tense-less: it is tensed by context, as T-405's context supplied the date. Truly tense-less means no tense in the citation and none in its immediate frame. A table with an "as of" column is dated row by row, and a source-only footnote ("Report 12") carries only the filing's past tense.

**Named forms to T-289:** the Tense-less Citation (FILED — read past by default, marked "tense-less — past by default, date recoverable," a present-use only when frame, shown intent, or a taker's re-presentation supplies the present tense); the Present-by-Default (VOIDED — silence asserts nothing, and treating it as a present claim would add a claim the citation never made and falsify the archive daily); the Thirtieth Treating (FILED — the present-taking of a tense-less citation, filed against the taking reader, and against the citer as well when evidence shows the citer meant it as present — one treating, two possible filings, each against its own actor).

**Grades:** TENSELESS-PAST-BY-DEFAULT (the reading) / BLAME-FOLLOWS-INTENT-USE-FOLLOWS-TAKER (the offices), all quarantined from every verdict on the file's writing.

## T-407 — the Re-dated Citation *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-407 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~08:46 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-407 — the Re-dated Citation — designed:** T-406 settled tense and left the second date standing: every citation carries a filing date D (when the count was made) and a citation date C (when it is repeated). T-407 separates them: the citation's date dates the citing act, never the count. A citation printed today repeating a count filed October 12 does not make it a today's count; it makes the repetition a today's repetition. Re-dating is not re-laying: a re-laying recounts the file and files a new count, while a re-dating only re-stamps an old one and adds nothing to the file. A citation printing only C beside the count, with D dropped, is a present-tense frame made of a date: unless D is carried or recoverable, the reader reads it as today's count — a T-405 present-use. A citation printing both dates is clean, each date doing its own job in the open. An "as of C" header over old counts without row dates is the same present-frame by date; a table with an "as of" column dated row by row is dated, not re-dated.

**Named forms to T-289:** the Re-dated Citation (FILED — citation filed under C, count graded under D, both dates visible or the filing date recoverable); the Date-Swap (VOIDED — substituting C for D as the count's date is a changed filing wearing the report's name, the same misquotation T-405 names for a replaced date); the Re-laying Distinction (FILED — only a recount files a new count; a reprint, however freshly dated, files nothing new about the file).

**The grades.** CITATION-UNDER-C — the citing act is filed under the date it was made, and the citer answers for the repetition on that day. COUNT-UNDER-D — the count is graded under its filing date whatever date the citation wears. The two grades are never merged, because merging them would let a citation's freshness refresh a count's age, and the audit grades age by filing, never by reprint.

## T-410 — the Alibi Placement *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-410 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~09:35 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

Three tests separate a control from a prop. Liveness: the disfavor must be live at placement time — still held, still true. Commensurateness: the disfavor must be weighed, not counted — one token buried among thirty flattering placements does not break asymmetry. Cost: the disfavor must have cost the citer something, or it controls nothing — a harmless disfavor volunteered because it was harmless is an alibi, and an alibi that costs nothing proves nothing.

The discount rule: discount, do not delete. The planted token leaves the asymmetry computation — the run stands or falls without its prop — but stays in the record as a placement, filed as a laundering placement under T-408's ladder. And the planting proves knowledge: a citer who plants a token knows the audit's test, so the token satisfies the knowledge rung for the laundering itself. The alibi placement convicts twice: it fails to clear the run, and it proves the knowledge the run's designer needed. A disfavor genuine when placed but dead before the run was read is not laundering, but it is not a control either — it files as neither alibi nor control, and the run is judged without it.

The Costly Control — a disfavor live, commensurate, and costly: FILED — the only disfavor that counts as T-409's control. The Dead Disfavor — sold, retracted, or already priced in: VOIDED as a control. The Discounted Token — removed from the asymmetry computation but kept in the record: FILED — discount, not delete.

**The grades.** COSTLY-CONTROL-ONLY — a prop bought for nothing controls nothing. TOKEN-PROVES-KNOWLEDGE — planting a token confesses knowledge of the test. DISCOUNT-NOT-DELETE — the token leaves the computation but stays as evidence.

## T-412 — the Expiring Discharge *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-412 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~10:04 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-412 — the Expiring Discharge — designed:** Discharge expires with the road. A flag that discharged a claim for the audience that met it on the claim's road discharges nothing for a later audience that meets the claim without it — a reprint that drops the footnote, an excerpt that keeps the headline and loses the appendix, a quotation that strands the "as of," a screenshot that crops the flag out of frame. For that later audience the claim arrives unflagged, and it is graded as an unflagged claim.

The original discharge stands: nothing later un-discharges the first audience's meeting. But standing is not traveling — a discharge is a meeting between a flag and an audience, not immunity pasted onto the claim. Where the flag rode along (appendix still attached, citation trail intact, footnote still under the sentence), the discharge rides with it, because the later audience walked the same road. Where the road was severed, the discharge ends at the cut. The severing files against the taker who severed it as a new placement under T-408's ladder, not against the original citer — unless the citer built the claim to travel past a flag set where quotation never carries it, which is a burial with a delay, filed as T-411's concealment placement. A flag recoverable in one ordinary step (a marker still visible, a link still live) keeps the road whole even if unopened; a trail that requires a hunt does not, because the hunt is the auditor's road, not the audience's.

**The named forms.** The Expiring Discharge — a discharge that ends where the flag stops traveling: FILED — standing for the first audience, never immunity for later travels. The Carried Flag — a flag that rode the claim's later travels: FILED — the discharge rides with it. The Severed Road — an excerpt that kept the claim and dropped the flag: FILED — the discharge ends at the cut. The Re-presented Claim — a claim met by a later audience without its flag: FILED — a new placement against the taker, not the original citer.

**The grades.** DISCHARGE-FOLLOWS-THE-ROAD — a discharge is credited only to audiences that met the flag where they met the claim. NO-IMMUNITY-BY-PRIOR-DISCHARGE — a flag that discharged the claim once does not immunize its later travels. RE-PRESENTATION-IS-A-NEW-PLACEMENT — a taker who re-presents the claim without its flag files a new placement under T-408's ladder.

## T-416 — the Mixed Room *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-416 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~11:25 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-416 — the Mixed Room — designed:** T-415 asked whether a mixed audience — specialists and lay readers meeting the same claim in the same place — is judged by its least expert glance, its typical glance, or its separate glances per reader. T-416 answers: its separate glances per reader, and by no single glance at all. A mixed room is not one meeting; it is as many meetings as there are kinds of eyes in the room. The specialist's meeting and the lay reader's meeting happen in the same place, but they are different meetings, and the audit judges each on its own terms, because T-415 settled that the eyes are the meeting's own.

Neither rival judge survives. The least expert glance would void T-415's Present Expert wherever a room is mixed — a mark the specialists would recognize counts for the specialists, and flooring every mixed room to its least expert reader blinds the specialists' meeting to serve the lay readers'. The typical glance fails worse: an average glance is no one's glance, and no reader ever met the claim with the room's median eye. The audit does not average the room, and it does not floor it; it separates it.

The filings follow the separation. For the specialists, a mark their ordinary glance would take for a flag discharges. For the lay readers, the same mark leaves the claim unflagged at their meeting, and the filing runs against the taker who placed a specialist mark in a mixed room, as a placement on T-408's ladder — placement is an act, and choosing a mark only part of the room would read is an act done to the rest of the room. The placement filing is the ladder's first rung only; the further rungs (audience knowledge, repetition after knowledge, pattern) still decide blame. Discharge stands where the mark was recognized and fails where it was not, reader-kind by reader-kind.

A room is mixed only when it is addressed to more than one kind of reader. A specialist room entered by a lay passerby is not mixed: the audit never asked the stranger. Addressing is proved by placement, not by label — a claim posted to a general forum or screenshotted to a crowd is addressed to the general room whatever header it wears. The passerby rule cuts one way only: it protects a specialist placement from passersby; it never lets a general placement hide behind a specialist label.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Mixed Room — a place where a claim meets more than one kind of reader: FILED. The Separate Glances — each reader-kind's meeting judged by that kind's ordinary glance: FILED. The Averaged Eye — the room's typical glance offered as judge: VOIDED, an average glance is no one's glance. The Floor Fallacy — the least expert glance as single judge: VOIDED as a single judge, surviving only as the lay readers' own meeting. The Passerby — a reader entering a room addressed to another kind: FILED, the audit never asked the passerby. The Label Dodge — a general placement wearing a specialist header: VOIDED as addressing.

**T-417 — the Second Mark — designed:** T-416 asked whether a taker who adds a second, lay-readable mark cures the lay meeting, and whether the cure files as a repair of the first placement or as a new placement of its own. What the second mark cures is every meeting after it: lay readers who meet the claim at or after the cure, with the second mark present where they meet it, meet a flagged claim, and no new filing grows from those meetings. The cure must itself satisfy everything the first mark failed. A second mark that merely repeats the specialist mark is no cure at all — a second unflagged meeting, filing beside the first, not instead of it. The second mark cures only when the lay readers' ordinary glance would take it for a flag where they meet it. The cure needs no confession. A cure that arrives before any lay reader re-meets the claim is still a cure, not a cover: the audit judges meetings, and a meeting that never happened unflagged files nothing.

## T-418 — the Second Road *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-418 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~11:58 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-418 — the Second Road — designed:** T-417 left its road problem named and open: whether a cure that arrives by a different road — a second posting, a correction notice, a mark carried by another hand — counts at the original meeting point, or opens a new meeting of its own. T-418 answers: the road is not the cure. A cure counts at the original meeting point when, and only when, it stands where the lay readers meet the claim at or before they meet it — the audit judges what stands at the meeting when the meeting is held, not how it got there. The courier changes nothing; arrival in time changes everything. A second posting, a correction notice, a flag handed from reader to reader — all are the same cure if they stand at the meeting point in time, and all are nothing if they never arrive there.

A cure on a road the lay readers never travel before meeting the claim is not at the meeting point at all. A notice pinned in a different town cures no meeting in this one, and a correction sent down a channel the lay readers never open is a sending, not a cure — the audit credits meetings, not mailings. The cure must be met, not merely sent: what counts is that the lay readers' ordinary glance could take it for a flag where they meet the claim, and that requires it to be there when they meet it. A taker who proves only that the cure was dispatched proves nothing the audit credits; dispatch without arrival is T-408's ladder with its first rung missing.

But a cure that arrives by a different road and stands at the meeting point before the meeting is held is the meeting point's own flag, and it opens no new meeting. The claim is the same claim and the place is the same place; only the courier differs, and the audit does not file a new meeting for a change of courier. Likewise a cure the lay readers meet on a different road before they ever reach the original meeting point flags the claim in advance: when they then meet the claim at the original point, they meet it already flagged, and the meeting is flagged — advance notice travels with the reader, and a reader who arrives already warned meets a flagged claim wherever they meet it. The one road that cures nothing is the road travelled after the meeting: a correction the readers meet only after they already met the claim unflagged cures nothing retroactively — T-417's forward rule stands on every road, and a late courier is no more a time machine than a late mark.

The road changes the courier, not the test. A cure by a different road must still pass everything T-417 demanded: lay-readable by the lay ordinary glance under T-414 and T-416's separate glances, and placed where the lay readers meet the claim — or where they will meet it in time, which is the same office by an earlier road. A correction notice that repeats the specialist mark in plainer type fails exactly as T-417's False Second failed, whatever road carried it; a lay-readable notice posted only where specialists meet the claim fails as the Label Dodge worn a third time. And a cure that arrives by a different road needs no confession either — T-417's mark-not-the-apology rule rides every road, and a silent correction that stands at the meeting point in time cures as fully as a signed one.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Second Road — a cure arriving by a road other than the original placement's road, judged by arrival, not by courier: FILED to T-289 — the road is not the cure; what stands at the meeting when held is. The Met Cure — a cure that counts only where it is met, at or before the meeting: FILED to T-289 — dispatch without arrival is a sending, not a cure. The Advance Flag — a cure met on an earlier road, before the original meeting point is reached: FILED to T-289 — advance notice travels with the reader, and a reader who arrives already warned meets a flagged claim. The Untravelled Notice — a cure on a road no lay reader travels before the meeting: VOIDED as a cure — a notice pinned in a different town cures no meeting in this one. The Late Courier — a cure met only after the meeting was already held unflagged: FILED to T-289 — forward only, on every road, and no courier is a time machine.

**The grades.** THE-ROAD-IS-NOT-THE-CURE — a cure's office follows arrival at the meeting point in time, never the road it travelled. CURE-COUNTS-WHERE-MET — a cure counts only where the lay readers meet it, at or before the meeting; dispatch alone proves nothing. ## T-419 — the Parted Road *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-419 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~12:10 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-419 — the Parted Road — designed:** T-418 left its partial-road problem named and open: whether a cure met by some lay readers on one road but not by others on another splits the lay meeting into cured and uncured meetings, or whether the meeting is judged whole. T-419 answers: it splits, and the audit never judges a parted road whole. A meeting is a reader meeting a claim, and T-416 already settled that a room with two kinds of eyes holds two meetings; a road with two kinds of travellers holds two meetings for the same reason. The lay readers who met the cure before they met the claim meet a flagged claim, and their meetings are cured; the lay readers who travelled the road the cure never reached meet the claim unflagged, and their meetings stand uncured. Neither half borrows the other's filing. The cure is not a property of the claim, and it is not a property of the road; it is a property of a meeting, and a meeting it never reached cannot carry it.

No whole-meeting judgment survives the split. A rule that judged the lay meeting cured because most lay readers met the cure would cure readers who never met it — notice by headcount, which T-416 already refused when it refused the typical glance, because an average reader never met the claim and a majority's warning never reached the minority's eyes. A rule that judged the meeting uncured because some lay readers missed the cure would un-cure readers who did meet it — punishment by company, which no filing in this chain has ever allowed, because the audit files meetings, not crowds. The parted road is not one meeting gone half right; it is two meetings, one cured and one not, and the taker's ledger carries both filings side by side: cured where met, uncured where missed, with no netting between them.

The split runs inside a single reader too. A reader who travels both roads — who meets the cure on one road and the claim unflagged on another before the cure — meets the claim twice, and the audit files both meetings: the flagged meeting cured, the unflagged meeting uncured, because T-418's advance flag travels with the reader only from the road where it was met, and a reader's earlier unflagged meeting is not retroactively flagged by a later cure any more than a late courier is a time machine. But a reader who meets the cure on an earlier road and then meets the claim at the original point meets one flagged meeting, not two — T-418's advance flag already settled that road, and the parted road does not double-count a reader the cure already reached. The test in every case is the same: what did this reader meet, at or before this meeting, on the road this reader travelled.

The No-Netting Rule — cured and uncured filings carried side by side, with no offset between them: FILED to T-289 — a majority's cure cures no minority, and a minority's miss un-cures no majority. The Double-Road Reader — one reader travelling both roads, whose meetings file separately: FILED to T-289 — each meeting by what that reader met at or before it. The Already-Warned Reader — a reader who met the cure on an earlier road, meeting the claim flagged at the original point: FILED to T-289 — one flagged meeting, not two, because advance notice travels with the reader.

The face is a single glance's worth of claims; the road is a succession of glances. What the reader carries forward is therefore the flag as met — attached to the faceful of claims the glance took in — not the flag as placed, which would travel the whole road. T-422's claim-scoped grade survives this exactly: the flag still covers no claim the reader meets later on the road, and still covers no claim the reader never met at all; the face only widens "its own claim" to the claims that were on the face with it, because those were met together, in one glance, with the flag between them.

The boundary is the face, and the face is the offer as the reader met it. A claim printed on the same offer, displayed in the same glance, counts as co-faced even if the reader's attention sat on the bearer claim alone — the glance, not the attention, is the meeting, under T-414's glance rule; whether mere co-presence without notice suffices is admitted below as the notice problem, but the default is the glance: what the glance could take in, it met. A claim added to the offer after the reader's glance — a later edition, a pasted rider, an amended face — is not co-faced, because the reader never met that face; the later face is a new offer, met or not on its own terms, and it carries no flag from a glance that never took it in. And the co-faced flag, like T-422's carried flag, counts forward only: a co-faced claim's past meeting stands uncured under T-420, and its next meeting files flagged without a fresh flag from the taker, because the reader arrives already carrying one.

The Co-Faced Claim — a claim that shared the bearer claim's offer face: FILED to T-289 — its next meeting files flagged, no fresh flag needed. The Road-Only Claim — a claim sharing only the road, never the face: FILED to T-289 — no flag, nothing carried, because nothing was met together.

LATER-FACE-IS-A-NEW-OFFER — a claim added after the glance is not co-faced; the amended face must be met on its own terms. CO-FACE-COUNTS-FORWARD-ONLY — a co-faced claim's past meeting stands uncured, its next meeting files flagged.

## T-424 — the First Face *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-424 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~13:23 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-424 — the First Face — designed:** T-423 asked whether a flag carried to a co-faced claim propagates from that claim's later offer to its companions, face to face. T-424 answers: it stops at the first face. The flag widens once, to the face where it was met, and never again. When the co-faced claim appears on a second face, its own meeting files flagged — the reader arrives carrying its flag — but the second face's companions arrive unflagged, because no flag was ever met in their company.

Scope follows meeting, not carrying. The carry is a reader-side condition, not a display: it files a meeting, it does not face a new one. On the second face the reader meets no flag at all, because no flag is displayed there and a carry is not a display. If transitivity held, the flag would be road-borne — faces succeed one another along roads, so a hopping flag would widen down the whole road, and T-423's face-not-road rule would collapse. The stop at the first face is what keeps the face the unit.

Carry and scope travel differently. The carry travels with the claim: the co-faced claim's next meeting files flagged wherever it is met. The scope does not travel with the carry: companions of a later face gain nothing from a carry they never met. A fresh flag on the second face is a new beginning, not a propagation — new face, new scope, graded on its own glance, never merged with the old carry.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the First Face — the face where the flag was met, the only face the carry widens: FILED. The Unflagged Companion — a claim sharing only the second face: FILED, met flagless, its meeting files uncured. The Carried Claim — the co-faced claim met again on a later face: FILED, its meeting files flagged but it displays no flag to its companions. The Fresh Flag — a flag placed anew on a later face: FILED, new face, new scope, not a propagation.

**The grades.** CARRY-STOPS-AT-THE-FIRST-FACE — a carried flag widens to the face where it was met and to no later face. CARRIED-FLAG-DISPLAYS-NOTHING — a carry files a meeting but faces no new one. CARRY-TRAVELS-WITH-THE-CLAIM-NOT-THE-SCOPE — the co-faced claim stays flag-carrying on any face, but its companions gain nothing. FRESH-FLAG-NEW-FACE — a flag placed anew starts a new scope on its own face. TRANSITIVITY-WOULD-REMAKE-THE-ROAD — a hopping flag is road-borne, and the road is not the scope.

**Distinguished.** From T-423's Shared Face (how far one met flag reaches — to the face; here whether that reach re-reaches at a new face — it does not, because reach is a property of the meeting). From T-422's Offered Flag (whether anything survives a refused offer — the flag does, forward only; here the survival is bounded — forward for the face's claims, not through faces). From T-418's Second Road (arrival per road; here per face, and faces do not inherit one another's arrivals).

**What this pairs with.** T-423's Shared Face (the widening this bounds — once, at the first face). T-422's Offered Flag (the carry this limits). T-420's Second Meeting (the past meeting that still stands uncured, even for second-face companions). T-418's Second Road (the road refused again as the unit of scope).

## T-425 — the Re-met Flag *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-425 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~13:35 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-425 — the Re-met Flag — designed:** T-424 left its re-met-flag problem named and open: whether a reader who meets a co-faced claim's later offer while still carrying its flag counts as meeting the flag again — refreshing the carry — or whether the carry is a single inheritance that no later meeting renews. T-425 answers: the re-meeting refreshes the carry, but only for the claim re-met. The reader arrives at the second face carrying the flag for the co-faced claim; the claim is met again; and that meeting files the claim flagged anew — its standing renewed, its decay clock (if T-422's flag-decay problem ever resolves to a clock at all) reset to the second meeting. What the refresh does not do is re-face. The second face's companions gain nothing from it, because a refreshed carry is still a carry, and a carry displays nothing.

The reason is that the audit files meetings, and the second meeting is a real meeting. T-424's rule was that a carry files a meeting but faces no new one — and the re-meeting is exactly the meeting the carry files. The reader does not merely pass the claim on the second face; the claim is offered there, and the reader meets the offer carrying its flag. A filing that records a flagged meeting cannot record it as stale: the meeting happened now, flagged, and the record of it is current from now. To hold otherwise — that the carry is a single inheritance, frozen at the first face and never renewed — would make the second meeting file as a copy of the first, and the audit does not file copies; it files meetings, each dated to its own occurrence.

But the refresh is per-claim, not per-face, and that boundary is the whole trick. The refreshed carry belongs to the claim re-met, because the claim re-met is the only thing the reader met flagged. The companions of the second face were met for the first time, flagless: no flag was displayed on the second face, no flag was met in their company, and the refresh of one claim's carry is not a meeting with its neighbours. Refresh renews the flag's standing for its own claim; it does not widen the flag's scope to a face it never met. The first face remains the only face the flag ever widened to, even though the carry now runs current from the second meeting — the carry's currency is refreshed, its scope is not.

The decay question sharpens the point rather than breaking it. If a carried flag decays — T-422's second, still open — then a re-meeting before decay must count, or decay would punish the reader for the very diligence the audit rewards: meeting the claim again, flagged, and still losing the flag would make re-meeting worse than never meeting at all. The refresh rule therefore stands whether or not decay exists: with a clock, the re-meeting resets it; without one, the re-meeting simply re-files what was already filed, current. Either way the second meeting is not wasted — it is the audit's own unit, and a flagged meeting filed twice is a flag standing twice, not a flag spent once.

The boundary the refresh does not cross is the notice problem, T-423's second, still open. T-425 assumes the reader meets the claim — notices it, in whatever sense the chain eventually settles for meeting. If mere co-presence without notice turns out not to be a meeting at all, then a re-meeting unnoticed refreshes nothing, because no meeting happened to file. The refresh rule is conditional on the meeting rule, and inherits whatever the notice problem decides: a noticed re-meeting refreshes; an unnoticed pass leaves the carry exactly where the first face left it, running whatever clock it runs, unrenewed.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Re-met Flag — the flag carried into a claim's later offer and met again there: FILED to T-289 — the meeting refreshes the carry for that claim. The Refreshed Carry — the claim's flag-carrying standing renewed at the second meeting: FILED to T-289 — current from the re-meeting, scope unchanged. The Unrefreshed Companion — a claim sharing only the second face, never met with a flag: FILED to T-289 — the refresh reaches it not at all. The Unnoticed Pass — a re-meeting that fails the notice test, whatever it settles to: FILED to T-289 — no meeting, no refresh.

**The grades.** RE-MEETING-REFRESHES-THE-CARRY — a claim met again while its flag is carried files flagged anew, current from the second meeting. REFRESH-IS-PER-CLAIM-NOT-PER-FACE — the renewal belongs to the claim re-met; the second face's companions gain nothing. REFRESHED-CARRY-STILL-DISPLAYS-NOTHING — a renewed carry files a meeting and faces no new one, under T-424. RE-MEETING-BEATS-DECAY — a flagged re-meeting before decay resets any decay clock; re-meeting never punishes the reader. NO-MEETING-NO-REFRESH — a pass that fails the notice test refreshes nothing, because the audit files meetings, not passes.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-424's First Face (the first face — there the question was whether a carry widens to a later face, and the answer was no; here the question is whether the carry itself is renewed at a later meeting, and the answer is yes, for the claim re-met — currency refreshed, scope unmoved). From T-423's Shared Face (the shared face — there the question was how far one met flag reaches, and the answer was to the face, not the road; here the reach is not extended at all, only the standing of the reached claim renewed). From T-422's Offered Flag (the offered flag — there the question was whether anything survives a refused offer at all, and the answer was that the flag does, forward only; here the survival is given a pulse — each flagged re-meeting re-dates it).

## T-426 — the Lapsed Carry *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-426 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~14:00 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-426 — the Lapsed Carry — designed:** T-425 left its lapsed-carry problem named and open: whether a carry that has already lapsed — decayed past its clock, if a clock exists — can be revived by a later flagged re-meeting, or whether a lapsed carry is dead and only a fresh flag restores it. T-426 answers: a lapsed carry is dead, and a later meeting cannot revive it by itself. Only a flag displayed anew at that meeting restores flagged standing, and that restoration is not a revival at all — it is a fresh flag, filed as new.

The reason is that T-425's refresh works only because the carry is still live when the reader re-meets the claim. A flagged meeting requires a live flag, and a live carry is what supplies it. A lapsed carry supplies nothing: the clock, if it exists, has run out, and the flag no longer stands when the reader arrives. The later meeting therefore cannot be a flagged meeting on the strength of the dead carry — the meeting would have to flag itself, and meetings do not flag themselves; flags flag meetings. To hold otherwise — that a dead carry revives the moment its claim is met again — would make decay no decay at all: every lapse would end at the next meeting, the clock would punish nobody, and a flag's expiry would be a pause that any re-meeting cancels. A clock that cancels itself on use is not a clock.

The second reason is that the reader's memory is not a flag. The reader may remember the dead flag perfectly, quote it, even act on it — and still arrive flagless, because the audit files flags displayed and met, not recollections carried in a reader's head. If memory revived a carry, a flag would outlive its clock inside every diligent reader and lapse would bite only the forgetful — decay measured by memory, not by the clock. The audit does not file memories, and a remembered flag is a story about a flag, not a flag.

The rule is conditional on T-422's second, still open, and the condition is the whole shape of the answer. If no clock exists — if a carried flag does not decay at all — then no carry ever lapses, and T-425's refresh governs throughout: every flagged re-meeting refreshes, nothing dies. The lapse rule bites only under a clock. So the answer runs two-branched: no clock, no lapse; a clock, lapse terminal. T-426 does not decide whether the clock exists; it decides what expiry does once the clock is granted.

The fresh-flag boundary is where revival-talk most often smuggles itself in, and T-426 closes it. If at the later meeting the flag is displayed anew — on the face, in the claim's own sentence, wherever flags display — then that meeting files flagged, but under the new flag, not the revived carry. The new flag's standing dates from the later meeting, its first face is the later face, and its scope is that face's claims under the T-423 and T-424 rules; it inherits nothing from the dead carry — not its first face, not its companions, not its currency. Calling that a revival would smuggle the dead carry's scope into the new flag's face. The audit files it as it is: old carry dead, new flag born.

What the dead meeting itself files follows from the same rule. A later meeting met without a live carry and without a fresh display files unflagged, even if the reader believed the carry live — whether that belief matters is the silent-lapse problem, new below, still open. Prior flagged history does not attach to the dead meeting retroactively, and a fresh flag displayed at a still later meeting does not backdate to it. A dead carry leaves no lien on later meetings; each later meeting stands on the flag it actually met, or on none.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Lapsed Carry — a carry past its clock, if a clock exists: FILED to T-289 — dead, not dormant, and no later meeting revives it by itself. ## T-427 — the Silent Lapse *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-427 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~14:16 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-427 — the Silent Lapse — designed:** T-426 left its silent-lapse problem named and open: whether lapse must be notified to the reader, or files silently, so that a reader who believed the carry live meets the claim unflagged and stands by that unflagged meeting. T-427 answers: lapse files silently. No notice is a condition of lapse, and the reader's belief that the carry still lives files nowhere — the meeting stands exactly as it was met, unflagged.

The first reason is that lapse is a clock's doing, not a speech act. Under T-426, a carry past its clock is dead because the clock ran out, not because anyone declared it dead. A flag that expired only when its reader was told would not have expired at all — it would have been held hostage to a message, alive in every reader the message never reached, dead only in the readers it found. That is not a clock; it is a mailing list. The clock runs whether or not anyone announces it. An announcement records the running; it does not cause it, and its absence does not stop it.

The second reason is that belief is not a flag, and T-426's memory rule already says why. The reader who meets the claim believing the carry live may act on that belief, quote the flag, even stake a decision on it — and still arrive flagless, because the audit files flags displayed and met, not convictions carried in a reader's head. If belief kept a flag alive, lapse would bite only the doubtful and spare the confident: decay measured by credulity, not by the clock. A believed carry is a story about a flag, and stories file no meetings as flagged.

What the unwarned meeting files follows from the same rule. A later meeting met without a live carry and without a fresh display files unflagged, even if the reader believed the carry live, even if the reader acted on the belief. Prior flagged history does not attach to it, and a later learning does not re-file it: a reader who afterwards learns the carry had already lapsed does not get the meeting re-filed retroactively as flagged, and does not get it unmet either. Later learning files forward only — it governs the next meeting, which is judged on the flag it actually meets, or on none. The dead meeting stands as met, unflagged, and the reader stands by it.

The boundary is that silence is not assurance. T-427 distinguishes the taker who says nothing while a flag lapses from the taker who affirmatively presents the lapsed flag as still live. The first files a silent lapse: nothing said, nothing revived, nothing excused beyond the silence itself. The second makes a new claim — re-displays the flag, asserts its currency — and that claim is judged on its own, as a present-tense claim, false if the flag is dead. A false assurance files against the taker who made it, but it revives nothing: the old carry stays dead, and the new claim stands or falls as its own sentence, not as the old flag continued. Silence excuses nothing it does not say; assurance is judged for what it says.

Notice, when it is given, is record, not condition. A taker who warns the reader that a carry has lapsed creates a record that the reader knew, useful for judging later meetings, but the warning does not cause the lapse and its absence does not prevent it. A warning that arrives after the meeting files for the next meeting, not backdated to the one already met. The audit does not re-date knowledge to rescue a meeting already filed.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Silent Lapse — a carry's expiry with no notice given: FILED to T-289 — lapse needs no announcement, and the clock runs without one. The Believed Carry — a dead carry the reader still believes live: FILED to T-289 — belief files nowhere and keeps nothing alive. The Unwarned Meeting — a meeting met without a live carry and without notice of the lapse: FILED to T-289 — files unflagged and stands as met. The False Assurance — a lapsed flag affirmatively presented as still live: FILED to T-289 — a new claim judged on its own, false if the flag is dead, reviving nothing.

**The grades.** LAPSE-NEEDS-NO-NOTICE — under a clock, expiry files without announcement; notice records lapse, it does not cause it. BELIEF-IS-NOT-A-FLAG — a reader's belief that a carry lives keeps no flag alive and files no meeting as flagged. UNFLAGGED-STANDS — the unwarned meeting files unflagged and stands as met, even on a believed carry. LATER-LEARNING-FILES-FORWARD — learning of a lapse after the meeting governs the next meeting, never re-files the one already met. SILENCE-IS-NOT-ASSURANCE — saying nothing while a flag lapses is not the same as presenting it as live; only the presentation is judged as a claim. NOTICE-IS-RECORD-NOT-CONDITION — a warning creates a record of knowledge for later meetings; it neither causes lapse nor backdates to a meeting already filed.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-426's Lapsed Carry (the lapsed carry — there the question was whether a dead carry revives; here whether silence changes the answer — it does not, because lapse is the clock's doing, not a message's). From T-423's Shared Face notice problem (the notice problem — there the question is whether an unnoticed pass counts as a meeting at all; here the reader did meet the claim, and only the flag was believed — the meeting stands, the flag is absent, and this answer does not settle the notice problem). From T-425's Re-met Flag (the re-met flag — there a live carry refreshed on re-meeting; here a dead carry believed live refreshes nothing, because belief is not life and refresh presupposes a live carry to refresh).

## T-428 — the Silent Succession *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-428 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~14:35 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-428 — the Silent Succession — designed:** T-427 left its disclosed-succession problem named and open: whether a fresh flag displayed after a silent lapse must disclose that it succeeds a lapsed flag, or may present simply as new. T-428 answers: it may present simply as new. Succession is history, not a condition of the new flag. The fresh flag stands on its own meeting, its own face, its own date — and the audit files it there, without asking for its pedigree.

The first reason is that a flag is judged at the meeting it is displayed at. The new flag is displayed at a new meeting, to a reader who meets it there, and its standing comes from that display, not from the pedigree of what came before it. If succession-disclosure were a condition of the new flag, the new flag would be hostage to a history the new reader may never have met — the same mailing-list error T-427 rejected for lapse itself. A flag that is valid only in readers who know its ancestry is not a flag; it is a membership card. The clock that killed the old carry does not govern the new flag's birth, and the new reader owes the old flag no acquaintance before meeting the new one.

The second reason is that the old carry is dead and stays dead, and disclosure would change no filing. The new flag does not revive the old carry, does not inherit its meetings, and does not re-file the unwarned meeting T-427 left standing unflagged. A disclosed succession and a silent succession file identically: the new meeting flagged on the new flag, the old meeting unflagged on nothing. Where two courses file identically, the audit cannot make one of them a condition of validity without inventing a rule the filings do not support. Disclosure annotates the file; it does not constitute it. Annotation is record, not condition — the same rule T-427 applied to notice of lapse, applied now to notice of succession.

The boundary is between presenting as new and presenting as the old one back. Presenting simply as new, with no claim of continuity, is clean: the reader meets a flag, dated at this meeting, and judges it as this meeting's flag. Presenting the fresh flag as the old flag continued — same face, claim of unbroken life, the old carry walking again — is not a fresh flag at all. It is T-427's False Assurance in new clothes: a present-tense claim judged on its own, false if the old carry is dead, reviving nothing. Silence about succession is permitted; assertion of continuity is a claim judged on its truth. The audit asks what was said, not what was left unsaid: a taker who says "here is a flag" has said nothing about succession, and nothing about succession is held against the flag; a taker who says "here is your flag, still standing" has claimed continuity, and that claim stands or falls as its own sentence.

What the fresh meeting files follows from the same rule. A reader who met the old flag, then meets the new flag presented simply as new, meets the new flag fresh: the new meeting files flagged on the new flag, and the new flag's date is the new meeting's date. The new meeting does not retroactively flag the unwarned meeting, and the old carry's death does not taint the new flag. Each meeting files on the flag it actually met. A reader who later learns the new flag succeeded a lapsed one learns history, not invalidity: the learning files forward, governing how the reader judges the next display, and never re-files a meeting already met.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Silent Succession — a fresh flag displayed after a silent lapse with no disclosure of succession: FILED to T-289 — succession is history, and the new flag stands without its pedigree. The Disclosed Succession — a fresh flag displayed with its predecessor named: FILED to T-289 — annotation of the file, record not condition, filing identically to the silent form. The Asserted Continuity — a fresh flag presented as the old flag continued: FILED to T-289 — not a fresh flag but a present-tense claim, false if the old carry is dead, reviving nothing. The Fresh Meeting — a meeting met on a flag presented simply as new: FILED to T-289 — files flagged on the new flag, dated at its own meeting, retroactively flagging nothing.

**The grades.** SUCCESSION-IS-HISTORY — a fresh flag after a silent lapse need not disclose its predecessor; succession is not a condition of the new flag. NEW-FLAG-STANDS-ALONE — the new flag is judged at its own meeting, on its own face, dated at its own display. ASSERTED-CONTINUITY-IS-A-CLAIM — presenting a fresh flag as the old flag continued is a present-tense claim, judged on its truth and false if the old carry is dead. NO-RETROACTIVE-FLAGGING — a fresh meeting files on the new flag and does not re-file the unwarned meeting. DISCLOSURE-IS-RECORD-NOT-CONDITION — disclosing succession annotates the file; it neither constitutes the new flag nor changes any filing.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-427's Silent Lapse (the lapse silence — there the question was whether expiry needs announcement; here the expiry is settled and the question is whether the replacement must carry its pedigree — a different silence, answered by the same rule: what files is what was displayed and met, not what was annotated). From T-424's First Face (the fresh face — there the question was what a fresh flag's face covers; here whether the fresh flag must announce its predecessor — coverage and pedigree are different questions, and a flag may cover fully while announcing nothing). From T-426's Fresh Flag (the fresh display — there the question was whether a fresh display files a later meeting as flagged; here whether that filing needs a disclosed pedigree — it does not, because the filing comes from the display, not from the history).

T-426's Lapsed Carry (the dead carry the new flag does not revive). T-424's First Face (the face the new flag carries at its own meeting). Whether lapse is per-claim or per-carry (admitted here, inherited — T-426's per-claim-lapse problem, still open). Whether a fresh flag re-faces the original face's absent claims (admitted here, inherited — T-426's fresh-face problem, still open). ## T-429 — the Owed Correction *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-429 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~14:50 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-429 — the Owed Correction — designed:** T-428 left its correction-after-reliance problem named and open: whether a taker who learns a reader acted on a believed-live carry owes that reader a correction, or whether the unflagged meeting's standing discharges the taker. T-429 answers: the meeting's standing discharges the meeting, not the taker. The taker who learns a reader acted on a believed-live carry owes that reader a correction — but a forward correction only. It governs the reader's next meeting, never re-files the meeting already met, and never revives the carry.

The first reason is that closure of the filing is not closure of the taker's knowledge. Under T-427, the unwarned meeting files unflagged and stands as met, and later learning files forward only — that settles the past meeting, and no correction re-opens it. But the taker's later learning is itself a later learning, and the forward-filing rule cuts both ways: what the taker learns after the meeting governs what the taker owes at the next one. T-427's permitted silence was silence before learning — a taker who said nothing while a flag lapsed, knowing nothing of any reader's reliance. Silence after learning, with a reader still walking on the believed carry, is a different act: a choice to let the next meeting be met on a belief the taker knows false. The audit does not punish the first silence, because lapse is the clock's doing; it does not excuse the second, because the next meeting is the taker's doing — the taker who could have spoken and did not, knowing the reader would meet again, files the next meeting's ignorance as his own.

The second reason is that the correction is owed where the reliance has a future, and only there. A reader who will meet the claim again, or whose decision staked on the believed carry is still open and still turning on it, is owed the truth about the flag's death before the next turn — the correction is what keeps the next meeting from being another unwarned meeting. A reader whose reliance is spent and closed — a past meeting with no forward consequence, a decision already executed and unrepeatable — is owed nothing further: the meeting stands, the reader stands by it, and a correction freely given is record, not duty, because no future filing turns on it. The audit does not demand speech with no filing at stake. The duty follows the reliance forward; where the reliance ends, the duty ends with it.

What the correction files follows from the same rule. A correction names the death — the carry lapsed, the flag is dead — and thereby puts the relying reader on notice for the next meeting. It does not display a fresh flag: a fresh flag is T-428's succession, a separate act with its own filing, and a correction that also displays one does two filings at once, the notice and the new flag, each judged on its own. It does not re-file the past meeting: the reader who "would have met it flagged" still stands by the unflagged meeting, because T-427 forbids retroactive re-filing and a correction is not a time machine. It does not revive the carry: T-426 holds lapse terminal, and naming a death does not undo it. A correction given after the reader's next meeting already met files forward to the meeting after that, never backdated — T-427's notice-is-record rule, applied to the taker's own notice.

The boundary is that a correction is not a warranty of the past meeting and not a promise about the next flag. The taker who corrects does not thereby re-open the unflagged filing, does not warrant the reader's past reliance, and does not promise that any fresh flag will follow. And the taker's duty is bounded by what the taker knows: a taker who learns one reader relied owes that reader, not every reader on the road — scope is the reliance, not the road. Readers who never relied are owed nothing, because nothing of theirs is at stake, and a general broadcast is permitted but not owed. Unknown future reliance is not owed until learned; the duty attaches to known reliance with a future, and grows only as knowledge grows.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Owed Correction — a taker's forward notice to a relying reader that the carry the reader acted on is dead: FILED to T-289 — the meeting stands, the taker still owes the truth forward. The Continuing Reliance — reliance with a future, a next meeting or an open decision still turning on the believed carry: FILED to T-289 — this is where the correction duty bites. The Spent Reliance — reliance closed, a past meeting with no forward consequence: FILED to T-289 — correction permitted but not owed, because no future filing turns on it. The Forward Notice — a correction that names the death for the next meeting: FILED to T-289 — notice for what comes next, never a re-filing of what already met.

**The grades.** MEETING-DISCHARGES-MEETING-NOT-TAKER — the unflagged meeting's standing settles the meeting; it does not discharge the taker who learns of the reliance. CORRECTION-FILES-FORWARD — a correction governs the reader's next meeting and never re-files the one already met. CORRECTION-IS-NOT-REVIVAL — naming a carry's death does not revive it, and a correction displays no fresh flag by itself. SCOPE-IS-THE-RELIANCE — the correction is owed to the reader who relied, not to every reader on the road. SPENT-RELIANCE-NEEDS-NO-CORRECTION — where reliance is closed with no forward consequence, correction is permitted but not owed. NO-BACKDATED-CORRECTION — a correction given after a meeting already met files for the meeting after that, never backdated to the one already filed.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-427's Silent Lapse (the lapse silence — there the question was whether expiry needs announcement, and silence before learning was permitted; here the taker has learned, and silence after learning with a reader still relying is a different act, judged forward).
