## T-430 — the Named Death *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-430 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~15:12 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-430 — the Named Death — designed:** T-429 left its correction's-form problem named and open: whether the correction must name the death, or whether displaying a fresh flag alone discharges the correction duty. T-430 answers: the correction must name the death. A fresh flag alone discharges nothing. The taker who learns a reader acted on a believed-live carry owes that reader a statement about the old carry's standing — that it lapsed, expired, was withdrawn, no longer stands — and a new display, however bright and however met, is not that statement.

The first reason is that a flag is a display and a correction is a sentence about the past, and the audit judges what was said, not what the taker hoped the reader would infer. "Here is a flag" says nothing about the old carry. A reader who meets a fresh flag may reasonably read it as an addition alongside the old one — a second flag, not a replacement — and keep walking on the believed carry for every claim and every open decision beyond the new flag's face. T-428's own rule cuts against the taker here: the audit asks what was said, not what was left unsaid, and a taker who said nothing about succession has said nothing the correction duty can credit. The fresh flag flags the next meeting on its face, and that filing stands; it does not warn the reliance, because warning is a different filing, and a display that never mentions the old carry cannot file it.

The second reason is that T-428's permission is not T-429's discharge, and the two filings must stay separate or one swallows the other. T-428 permitted a fresh flag to present simply as new — that permission was granted to the flag, for the flag's own standing, and it says nothing about the taker's duty to a reader who relied. If a bare flag discharged the correction duty, every succession would silently settle every reliance, and the correction duty would exist only where the taker chose not to display a flag — a duty conditioned on the taker's convenience, not on the reader's reliance. T-429 kept the filings separate on purpose: a correction that also displays a flag does two filings at once, the notice and the new flag, each judged on its own. T-430 holds the converse with the same rule: a flag that displays no notice does one filing only, and the notice filing remains undone, however complete the flag filing is.

What counts as naming follows from the same rule: substance fixed, wording free. Naming must be a statement about the old carry's standing — that it lapsed, expired, was withdrawn, was replaced, no longer stands. It need not use the word "death": any plain statement that leaves no reasonable reading under which the old carry still stands names it. A display captioned "this replaces the earlier flag" names the death, because replacement says the old no longer stands, and the caption is judged as part of what was said. A bare display does not, even on the same face as the old claim, because a display alone asserts nothing about what came before it. A caption praising the new flag — "a stronger flag," "a new flag here" — does not name it either, because praise of the new says nothing about the standing of the old. The audit asks whether the old carry's standing was stated, not whether the new flag was displayed well.

What the correction's form files follows from the same rule. A reader who meets the fresh flag but never hears the death is flagged for the next meeting on the new face and unwarned for everything beyond it: the next meeting files flagged on the new flag, while the open decisions still turning on the believed carry remain unwarned, and the correction duty stands undischarged for that reliance. Discharge is per-reliance, not per-display: a flag met by the reader discharges nothing beyond the meetings its own face covers, and the duty is measured by the reliance warned, not by the displays made. A taker who both names the death and displays a fresh flag does two filings at once under T-429's rule, and neither taints the other — the naming does not weaken the flag, and the flag does not weaken the naming. And naming the death, by itself, displays no flag: the warned reader's next meeting still files unflagged until a fresh flag is displayed, because naming warns while only display flags, and a warning is not a flag.

The boundary is between discharge and mootness, and the audit must not credit the flag for what ended the reliance. Where the reliance ends before any naming — the reader's decision executed, the future closed, T-429's spent reliance — the correction duty ends with it, and the duty is mooted, not discharged: the flag did not satisfy the duty, the reliance simply stopped asking anything of it. A taker who points at the flag and claims discharge for a spent reliance claims credit for time's work, not his own. Discharge means the relying reader was told the old carry died while the reliance still had a future; mootness means the future ran out first. Both leave the taker owing nothing further, but only the first is the duty performed, and the file must say which one it was.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Named Death — a correction that states the old carry's standing, that it lapsed, expired, was withdrawn, or no longer stands: FILED to T-289 — substance fixed, wording free, and the only form that discharges the correction duty. The Bare Flag — a fresh flag displayed with no statement about the old carry: FILED to T-289 — it flags the next meeting on its face and discharges nothing. The Replacing Caption — a fresh flag captioned "this replaces the earlier flag" or its plain equivalent: FILED to T-289 — replacement states the old no longer stands, so the caption counts as naming. The Second-Flag Fallacy — reading a fresh flag as proof the old carry died: VOIDED — a display asserts nothing about what came before it, and inference is not naming. The Mooted Duty — a correction duty ended because the reliance closed before naming: FILED to T-289 — the duty ended, but it was not discharged by any flag.

**The grades.** NAME-THE-DEATH — a correction discharges only when it states the old carry's standing; a fresh flag alone discharges nothing. BARE-FLAG-DISCHARGES-NOTHING — a display with no statement about the old carry files the next meeting flagged and warns no reliance. SUCCESSION-PERMISSION-IS-NOT-DISCHARGE — T-428's permission for a flag to present as new was granted to the flag, not to the taker's duty. NAMING-IS-ABOUT-THE-OLD — naming must speak of the old carry's standing; praise of the new flag does not name the old one's death. WORDING-FREE-SUBSTANCE-FIXED — any plain statement leaving no reasonable reading of continued life counts; no single word is required. DISCHARGE-IS-PER-RELIANCE — discharge is measured by the reliance warned, not by the displays made. NAMING-WARNS-DISPLAY-FLAGS — naming warns the reliance, only display flags the next meeting, and neither act substitutes for the other. MOOTED-IS-NOT-DISCHARGED — a duty ended by the reliance closing is mooted, not performed, and the file must say which.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-429's Owed Correction (the correction owed — there the question was whether the taker owes a correction at all once he learns of the reliance; here the question is what form satisfies a duty already owed — existence and form are different questions, and a duty whose form is a bare flag is no duty at all). ## T-431 — the Unmet Correction *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-431 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~15:20 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-431 — the Unmet Correction — designed:** T-430 left its unmet-correction problem named and open: whether a correction delivered but never read discharges the duty, or whether the duty persists until the relying reader meets the naming, and whether naming must be met in the ordinary glance like a flag. T-431 answers: the duty persists until the naming is met in the ordinary glance, and delivery alone discharges nothing. A correction the relying reader never met is a correction the audit does not credit, however properly the taker sent it — and a correction the ordinary glance meets is met, whether or not the taker's proof can show this reader's eyes landing on the words.

The first reason is that a correction is a sentence addressed to a reader, and the audit judges what reached the reader's path, not what left the taker's hands. T-430 fixed the correction's form: it must name the death, substance fixed, wording free. Form without arrival is a sentence spoken into an empty room. A naming posted to a drawer the reader never opens, filed in an annex the reader never visits, or sent down a channel the reader never glances at says nothing to that reader, and the audit credits sentences said, not sentences sent. The taker who points at his own outbox and claims discharge claims credit for his own act, not for the reader's warning — and the correction duty was owed to the reader's reliance, so only the reader's meeting can satisfy it. Delivery is the taker's motion; meeting is the correction's arrival; the duty ends at arrival, never at motion.

The second reason is that the ordinary glance is already the chain's shared standard for meeting, and the correction inherits it rather than inventing its own. T-414's glance rule judges a flag by what the ordinary glance meets on the face, and T-422 carried a flag forward on exactly that meeting — met on the face in the ordinary glance, carried; unmet, carried nothing. The naming travels the same path to the same reader, so it is judged by the same glance: met means placed where the reader's ordinary glance meets it — on the face the reader ordinarily meets, in the channel the reader ordinarily reads — and not met means placed anywhere else. Requiring proof of actual reading would make discharge unprovable in every case, since no taker can exhibit another reader's eyes; requiring mere sending would make discharge automatic in every case, since every taker can exhibit his own outbox. The ordinary glance is the middle standard the chain already trusts: it asks where the naming stood, not whether the reader looked, and it refuses both the unprovable and the automatic.

What counts as met follows from the same rule: placement on the ordinary path, judged by the reader's ordinary route, not the taker's convenience. A naming captioned on the face the reader meets when the claim comes up is met, because the ordinary glance meets the face. A naming buried in an appendix the reader's route never opens, tucked into a second envelope the reader never unseals, or filed under a heading the reader's glance skips is unmet, because the ordinary glance never meets it — however plain the wording, however correct the substance. T-430's substance rule and T-431's meeting rule judge different halves of the same filing: the naming must both say the death and stand where the glance meets it, and either half missing leaves the filing undone. A perfectly worded naming in an unglanced drawer is as undischarged as a bare flag on the open face: one fails arrival, the other fails content, and the duty persists under both.

What the unmet naming files follows from the same rule. An unmet naming files nothing: the correction duty persists in full, the reader's reliance stays unwarned, and the reader's next meeting files exactly as it would have without the naming — unflagged unless a fresh flag is displayed, because naming warns while only display flags, under T-430's rule. The taker who learns the naming went unmet owes a fresh naming, by the same logic that T-429's learning of the reliance created the duty in the first place: learning is the trigger, and learning that the cure never arrived re-triggers it. But the presumption runs the other way while the taker learns nothing: a naming placed on the ordinary path is presumed met, and the duty stands discharged on that presumption, until the taker learns it went unmet. A reader's bare denial — "I never saw it" — is not by itself that learning: denial without more is a claim about the reader's eyes, and the audit judges placement, not eyes. Knowledge that reopens the duty means knowledge of the placement's failure — misdelivery proven, a wrong address, a dead channel, a face the reader's route never meets — not a reader's say-so after the fact. Suspicion does not reopen; knowledge does.

The boundary is between mootness and persistence, and the audit must not confuse a duty still owed with a duty already ended. Where the reliance closes before the naming is met — the reader's decision executed, the future closed, T-430's spent reliance — the duty is mooted, not discharged and not persisting: there is no longer a reliance for any naming to warn, so nothing is owed and nothing is credited. Where the reliance still has a future and the naming stands unmet, the duty persists, and it persists no matter how long the naming has sat in the drawer: time does not convert an unmet naming into a met one, and the drawer does not become the ordinary path by aging. A taker who waits out an unmet naming and then claims the reliance must have met it by now claims credit for the calendar, not for the correction. Only meeting ends the duty; only mootness ends it without meeting; and the file must say which one it was.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Met Naming — a correction naming the death and placed where the reader's ordinary glance meets it: FILED to T-289 — the only form that discharges the correction duty. The Unmet Naming — a correction naming the death but placed where the ordinary glance never meets it: FILED to T-289 — it discharges nothing, and the duty persists in full. The Drawer Letter — a naming delivered to a channel the reader never glances at, however properly sent: FILED to T-289 — delivery is the taker's motion, meeting is the correction's arrival. The Ordinary-Path Placement — a naming standing on the face or in the channel the reader ordinarily meets: FILED to T-289 — placement on the ordinary path is what meeting means. The Presumed Meeting — a naming on the ordinary path credited as met without proof of reading: FILED to T-289 — the audit judges placement, not eyes. The Reopened Duty — a correction duty revived by the taker's learning that the naming went unmet: FILED to T-289 — learning re-triggers what sending never finished. The Bare Denial — a reader's unsupported "I never saw it" offered as reopening: VOIDED — denial without knowledge of placement's failure does not reopen a presumed meeting.

**The grades.** DELIVERY-DISCHARGES-NOTHING — a correction sent but never met credits nothing; the duty persists until the naming is met. MEETING-IS-THE-ORDINARY-GLANCE — naming must be met in the ordinary glance like a flag, judged by T-414's standard, not by proof of reading. PLACEMENT-NOT-EYES — the audit asks where the naming stood on the reader's ordinary path, never whether this reader's eyes landed on it. PRESUMED-UNTIL-KNOWN-OTHERWISE — a naming on the ordinary path stands met until the taker learns its placement failed. KNOWLEDGE-REOPENS — learning that a naming went unmet re-triggers the duty, as learning of the reliance created it. DENIAL-IS-NOT-KNOWLEDGE — a bare denial reopens nothing; only knowledge of placement's failure does. MOOTED-IS-NOT-PERSISTING — a reliance closed before meeting moots the duty; a reliance still open keeps it persisting, however long the naming has waited.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-430's Named Death (the correction's form — there the question was what a correction must say, naming the death with substance fixed and wording free; here the question is whether saying it counts before the reader meets it, and form without arrival counts for nothing — content and arrival are different halves of one filing, and either half missing leaves it undone). From T-422's Offered Flag (the carried flag — there the question was whether a flag met on a refused offer's face carries into future meetings; here the question is whether a naming met on the reader's path discharges a duty already owed — carrying looks forward to the next meeting, discharge looks backward to the reliance warned, and the two rules judge different directions). From T-414's glance rule (the standard inherited — there the glance judged whether a flag was met; here the same glance judges whether a naming was met — the standard is borrowed whole, not remade, because the naming travels the flag's path to the same reader).

**What this pairs with.** T-430's Named Death (the form this meeting completes — naming the death is the content, meeting in the ordinary glance is the arrival). T-429's Owed Correction (the duty this meeting discharges — forward only, scoped to the reliance, reviving nothing and re-filing nothing). T-422's Offered Flag (the carry judged by the same glance — met on the face, carried forward; unmet, carried nothing). T-414's glance rule (the standard itself — what the ordinary glance meets is what counts as met). T-427's Silent Lapse (the lapse whose silence before learning was permitted, and whose naming after learning must still arrive to count).

**Admitted-unsolved carried forward.** Whether a second naming, after the first goes unmet, must travel a different channel than the failed one, or whether re-placement on the same ordinary path suffices (admitted here, new — the second-channel problem). Whether a reader's denial, once the taker believes it, counts as the knowledge that reopens the duty, or whether belief without placement evidence still reopens nothing (admitted here, new — the believed-denial problem). Whether a fresh flag re-faces the original face's absent claims (admitted here, inherited — T-426's fresh-face problem, still open). Whether a carried flag decays at all, and whether a misread flag carries forward (admitted here, inherited — T-422's second and third, still open). Whether co-faced coverage needs notice, and whether a face split across folds counts as one face (admitted here, inherited — T-423's second and third, still open). Whether a verbatim reprint re-faces claims with the old flag, and whether a taker owes flags for a new face's companions (admitted here, inherited — T-424's second and third, still open). ## T-432 — the Second Naming *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-432 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~15:38 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-432 — the Second Naming — designed:** T-431 left its second-channel problem named and open: whether a second naming, after the first goes unmet, must travel a different channel than the failed one, or whether re-placement on the same ordinary path suffices. T-432 answers: the second naming must travel the reader's ordinary path as corrected by what the taker learned — and that correction decides the channel. Where the learning shows the channel itself was not the reader's ordinary path, the same channel is void for the second naming and a different, actually-ordinary channel is required. Where the learning shows only that one instance failed on a sound path, re-placement on the same path suffices. Where the learning shows failure but not cause, the second naming must differ in placement from the failed one — repetition of the identical failed placement is not a fresh placement at all.

The first reason is that T-431's meeting rule judges placement by the reader's ordinary route, not by the taker's label, and the taker's learning changes what that route is known to be. A channel the taker now knows the reader never meets — a dead channel, a wrong address, a face the reader's route never opens — is not the ordinary path with a blemish on it; it is a drawer the taker has now identified as a drawer. T-431 called the first such placement the Drawer Letter and filed it as discharging nothing. A second placement in the same identified drawer is the same filing twice: the taker learned the placement failed, then repeated the placement he learned had failed, and claims the second attempt counts because it is second. The audit counts placements, not attempts. The second naming earns its presumption only by standing somewhere the reader's route actually meets — the corrected path — and a channel known not to be that path cannot earn it. Knowledge defeats presumption on that channel: the presumption T-431 granted ran on placement on the ordinary path, and a channel now known not to be the ordinary path is outside the presumption's grant, however often the taker posts to it.

The second reason is that the distinction between route failure and instance failure is the distinction between a broken road and a lost letter, and the audit must not treat them alike in either direction. A letter lost in a good channel — misfiled once, misdelivered once, dropped once — leaves the channel sound: the reader's ordinary route still runs through it, and the failure was the instance, not the route. Re-placement on the same path then suffices, because the path is still the ordinary path and the second placement is a genuine fresh placement on it, entitled to the same presumed-met standing the first would have had. To demand a different channel after every instance failure would punish sound routes for accidents and drive the taker off the reader's ordinary path onto stranger channels the reader meets less — the opposite of what the correction duty wants. But the converse error is worse: to permit re-placement on a failed route treats a known drawer as a path and lets the taker discharge his duty by posting twice into the void. The rule follows the learning: the second naming must correct what the learning corrected — the route where the route failed, the instance where only the instance failed.

The third reason covers the case where the taker learns the naming went unmet but not why — the reader's reliance still unwarned, the placement's failure known, its cause unknown. There the second naming must differ in placement from the failed one: a different face, a different channel, or a different caption on the same face that puts the naming where the glance cannot skip it. Repetition of the identical placement, with no knowledge of why it failed, is not a fresh placement but a wager that the same placement will succeed this time for no reason the taker can state — and the audit credits placements, not wagers. The difference need not be a different channel: a naming moved from an annex heading the glance skips to the face the claim comes up on differs in placement even within one channel, because placement is judged by the glance's route, not by the channel's name. What the unknown-cause case forbids is the identical placement repeated unchanged: same drawer, same heading, same tuck — a second drawer letter wearing the first one's address.

What counts as a sufficient second naming follows from the three cases, and the file must show which case it is. Route failure: a different channel, actually ordinary, with the learning stated — the old channel named as failed as a route, the new channel shown as the reader's route. Instance failure: the same path re-placed, a fresh instance, with the learning stated — the path shown still sound, the failure shown as the instance's. Unknown cause: a placement differing from the failed one in face, channel, or caption, with the difference shown, not merely claimed. In all three cases the second naming must still name the death — T-430's content rule is unchanged by the second attempt, and the second naming's content is the death, not its predecessor's failure; narrating the first failure is permitted, never required. And in all three cases the second naming, once it stands on the corrected path, earns T-431's presumed-met standing in full: a taker who has learned one failure does not labor under a permanent suspicion, and the second naming is presumed met until new learning, exactly as the first was. What the taker loses by learning is narrower and exact: he loses the presumption on the failed channel only, and only where the learning showed the route failed. Suspicion about other channels does not follow; knowledge does not generalize beyond what it showed.

What the insufficient second naming files follows from the same rule. A second drawer letter files as the first did — duty persisting in full, reliance still unwarned, the reader's next meeting filing exactly as it would have without any naming, unflagged unless a fresh flag is displayed, because naming warns while only display flags, under T-430's rule. And the file must record the sequence: that the first naming went unmet, what the taker learned, and what the second naming corrected — because a file showing two placements on the same channel with no account of the first failure reads as a single placement counted twice, and the audit judges the file it is given. Whether that record is itself a filing the duty requires, or merely good file-keeping, is admitted below as the failure-record problem, left open.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Second Naming — a correction naming the death, placed on the reader's ordinary path as corrected by what the taker learned from the first naming's failure: FILED to T-289 — the only form that discharges a duty already reopened once. The Route Failure — a first naming failed because its channel was not the reader's ordinary path: FILED to T-289 — the channel is void for the second naming, and a different, actually-ordinary channel is required. The Instance Failure — a first naming failed as one instance on a sound path: FILED to T-289 — re-placement on the same path suffices, because the path is still the ordinary path. ## T-433 — the Escalation *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-433 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~15:48 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-433 — the Escalation — designed:** T-432 left its escalation problem named and open: whether a third naming, after two failures, must escalate beyond corrected-path placement — direct hand delivery, witnessed receipt, or some stronger arrival — or whether corrected-path placement suffices indefinitely, however many namings fail. T-433 answers: the third naming must escalate, and the escalation is a change of kind, not of force. After two failures, the ordinary-path presumption itself is spent: the taker may no longer discharge his duty by placing a naming where the reader is presumed to meet it, because the road has now twice shown the presumption wrong. The third naming must therefore be met in fact, not presumed met — its meeting shown by the reader's own act or by a witness to the delivery, not inferred from placement on any path, however corrected. Corrected-path placement suffices for the first naming and, corrected again, for the second; it does not suffice for the third, because the third naming is no longer a placement on a road presumed sound — it is a delivery to a reader whose road has twice failed to carry it.

The first reason is that T-432's corrected path was a repair, not a renewal, and repairs run out. The first naming earned presumed-met standing from placement on the ordinary path. The second naming earned the same standing from placement on the path as corrected by what the first failure taught. But each failure teaches something the correction cannot un-teach: that the taker's knowledge of the reader's ordinary route is now twice wrong. After the first failure, the taker could still say the route was sound and the instance failed, or the channel was wrong and another was right — in either case a corrected path remained a path the reader could be presumed to meet. After the second failure, that sentence no longer holds: the corrected path has itself failed, so the taker's map of the reader's route is not merely imperfect, it is twice disproven. A third placement on yet another corrected path would be a third wager on a map that has lost twice — and T-432 already ruled that placements, not wagers, are what the audit credits. The presumption that made placement count as meeting was granted on the road's presumed soundness; two failures on the road, original and corrected, spend that grant. What remains is not a worse placement but a different standard: meeting shown, not meeting presumed.

The second reason is that escalation is about the proof, not the muscle. Direct hand delivery, witnessed receipt, a signed acknowledgement, the reader's own later act that shows the naming was met — these are not stronger versions of placement; they are arrivals whose meeting does not depend on the taker's map at all. A hand-delivered naming counts because the hand was seen to arrive, not because the hand is forceful; a witnessed receipt counts because the witness saw the reader take it, not because the witness is authoritative. The escalation rule therefore does not require any particular ritual, and it forbids none: any arrival whose meeting is shown rather than presumed satisfies it, and no placement, however careful, however corrected, however repeated, satisfies it by placement alone. That is why the rule is not "try harder" — harder placement on a twice-failed map is still placement, and the audit's objection to the third placement is not that it is weak but that its standing would still rest on presumption. Force without proof is a louder drawer letter; proof without force is a quiet hand that arrived.

The third reason sets the limit on both sides, because an escalation rule without a limit becomes either an infinite ladder or an excuse to stop. The limit on the taker's side: the third naming must be met in fact, but the taker need not produce the reader — he must produce meeting, and meeting can be shown by the reader's act as well as by a witness. A reader who, after the third naming, acts in a way only a reader who met the naming would act — withdrawing the reliance, correcting the next meeting, citing the death — has met it, and the file may show that act as the proof. A reader who merely could have met it has not, and the file must not dress possibility as proof. The limit on the reader's side: the duty persists through the third naming's failure as it persisted through the first two — an unmet third naming does not discharge, and it does not convert the duty into a discharged one by exhaustion. What the third failure changes is not the duty's existence but the taker's route forward: a fourth naming must also be met in fact, and the taker must not fall back to placement, because the presumption, once spent, does not revive by waiting. The ladder has one rung of escalation — from presumed to proven — and then stays there: every naming after the second must be proven, however many it takes, until one is met.

What counts as a sufficient third naming follows from the three reasons, and the file must show which proof it is. A witnessed arrival: the delivery seen by a witness who can say the reader took it, with the witness named and the taking shown, not merely the posting. A reader's acknowledgement: a signed receipt, a reply, or any act of the reader's that answers the naming itself, with the answer shown. A reader's consequential act: conduct after the naming that only a met reader would show, with the conduct stated and the inference from it stated, not merely asserted. In all three cases the third naming must still name the death — T-430's content rule is unchanged by escalation, and the proof goes to the meeting, not to the wording; a perfectly proven delivery of a bare flag proves only that a flag was delivered, and discharges nothing, because T-430's naming rule stands. And in all three cases the proof, once shown, discharges in full: a proven third naming needs no fourth, and the duty ends by meeting, not by the count of attempts.

What the insufficient third naming files follows from the same rule. A third corrected-path placement, however thoughtful the correction, files as the second drawer letter did — duty persisting in full, reliance still unwarned, the reader's next meeting filing exactly as it would have without any naming, unflagged unless a fresh flag is displayed, because naming warns while only display flags, under T-430's rule. A third naming proven only by the taker's insistence — "I delivered it by hand" with no witness, no receipt, no consequential act — files as a claim of proof, not as proof, and the audit judges the file it is given. Whether the file must also record the two failures and their corrections — the record T-432 left open — is admitted below as the failure-record problem, left open.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Escalation — a third naming, after two failures, that must be met in fact rather than presumed met: FILED to T-289 — the only form that discharges a duty already reopened twice. The Spent Presumption — the presumed-met standing lost when the corrected path itself fails: FILED to T-289 — after two failures, placement no longer earns presumption, on any channel. The Proven Meeting — a naming whose meeting is shown by the reader's act or a witness's seeing: FILED to T-289 — proof replaces presumption from the third naming onward. The Witnessed Arrival — a delivery seen to reach the reader's hands: FILED to T-289 — the witness's seeing is the proof, not the witness's authority. The Consequential Act — conduct after the naming that only a met reader would show: FILED to T-289 — the reader's act proves the meeting the placement could not. The Unrevived Presumption — the standing that does not return by waiting or by a third correction: FILED to T-289 — once spent, presumption stays spent until a naming is proven. The Louder Drawer — a third placement, however forceful or corrected, whose standing would still rest on presumption: VOIDED — it discharges nothing; force without proof is not arrival.

**The grades.** PRESUMPTION-SPENDS-AFTER-TWO — two failures, original path and corrected path, spend the presumed-met grant; a third placement earns no presumption. ESCALATION-IS-PROOF-NOT-FORCE — the third naming must be met in fact, by witness, acknowledgement, or consequential act, not by stronger placement. PROOF-REPLACES-PLACEMENT — from the third naming onward, meeting must be shown, never inferred from where the naming stood. PROVEN-DISCHARGES-IN-FULL — one proven third naming ends the duty; the count of attempts is not the discharge. UNMET-THIRD-PERSISTS — a failed third naming leaves the duty exactly where the first two left it, and no fallback to placement follows. From T-430's Named Death (the correction's content — there the question was what a correction must say, naming the death with substance fixed and wording free; here the question is how the saying must arrive, and content rules do not answer arrival rules — a perfectly worded third naming placed on a third corrected path fails exactly as the first two did, for the new reason that its standing would rest on a spent presumption).

## T-434 — the Disinterested Witness *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-434 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~16:10 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-434 — the Disinterested Witness — designed:** T-433 left its witnessed-proof problem named and open: what counts as proof of meeting — whether a witness's word alone suffices, or the witness must be disinterested, or the reader's signature alone suffices, or only the reader's consequential act proves meeting beyond the witness's say-so. T-434 answers: a disinterested witness suffices, and nothing else on the witness side does. The witness's word alone does not suffice, because a word is only as good as the mouth it comes from, and T-433's escalation replaced a presumption about a road with a proof about a meeting — not with a new presumption about a person. An interested witness's word is the taker's word in another mouth, and the audit does not credit it twice because it was spoken twice. A disinterested witness's seeing is different in kind: he gains nothing and loses nothing by the naming counting as met, he was given no instruction about what to see or report, and what he states is the taking itself, not the posting. The reader's signature alone does not suffice either, because a mark on paper claimed to be the reader's is a claim about a hand, not a hand shown; a signature suffices only when it is authenticated as the reader's and identifies the naming it receipts. And the reader's consequential act is sufficient without any witness at all — but it is not required on top of a disinterested witness, because T-433's ladder has one rung, and demanding both a witness and an act would quietly add a second.

The first reason is that a witness, unless disinterested, merely moves the presumption. T-433 spent the ordinary-path presumption after two failures: placement no longer earns presumed-met standing, on any channel. If any witness's word restored that standing, the spending would be undone by hiring — the taker could buy back, for the price of a friendly mouth, exactly the presumption the two failures spent. The audit therefore asks of every witness what the road can no longer be asked: what do you gain or lose if this naming counts as met? A witness who is the taker's agent, who is paid by the outcome, whose standing improves when the duty counts discharged, or who was instructed by the taker to report a meeting, is interested, and his word files as the taker's claim, not as proof — however confident, however detailed, however often repeated. Two interested witnesses do not sum to one disinterested witness, because addition of claims is still claim; ten voices saying what the taker paid them to say are one voice with an echo. Disinterest is judged by stake in the outcome, not by character, friendship, or familiarity: a stranger summoned by the taker can be disinterested if he has no stake and no instruction, and a familiar face can be disinterested if the naming's counting as met neither gains nor loses him anything. What disqualifies is not closeness but interest — a hand in the outcome, or an instruction about what the hand should report.

The second reason is that the witness must state a taking, not a posting, and the signature must be authenticated, not merely shown. A witness who saw the naming posted, left, laid on a desk, or handed to a household does not prove meeting, however disinterested he is: posting is placement, and placement is exactly what T-433 ruled insufficient after two failures. The disinterested witness must be able to say the reader took it — took the naming into his hands, received it, acknowledged it to the witness's face — with the witness named, the taking stated, and the naming identified, so the file shows what was taken and by whom, not merely that something arrived somewhere. The signature rule follows the same line: a signature proves a meeting only when the file shows whose hand made it and what it signed. A mark claimed to be the reader's, on a receipt that does not identify the naming, proves neither hand nor meeting. An authenticated signature — matched to a known exemplar of the reader's hand, made in a disinterested witness's seeing, or later adopted by the reader as his own — on a receipt identifying the naming, proves the taking as surely as a witness's seeing, because the hand shown is the reader's and the paper signed is the naming. Authentication goes to the hand, identification goes to the paper; either missing, the signature files as a claim of acknowledgement, not as acknowledgement.

The third reason sets the limit on both sides, because a proof rule without a limit becomes either a demand for two proofs or an excuse to accept none. The limit on the taker's side: one sufficient proof discharges, and the taker need not stack proofs. A disinterested witness's stated taking needs no consequential act beside it, and a consequential act needs no witness beside it — the reader who, after the naming, acts in a way only a met reader would act has met it, and the file may show that act as the proof, with the conduct stated and the inference from it stated, not merely asserted. Demanding witness plus act would be a second rung on T-433's one-rung ladder, and T-433 already ruled the ladder stays at proven meeting, however many attempts it takes. The limit on the reader's side: a bare denial does not undo a stated taking. A reader who says he never met the naming files a denial beside the witness's seeing, and the audit judges the file it is given — but denial alone does not erase proof, any more than proof alone erases denial. What undoes a witness's proof is a showing, in the file, that the witness was interested after all, or that what he saw was a posting rather than a taking; what undoes an authenticated signature is a showing that the hand was not the reader's, or the paper signed was not the naming. Until such a showing is filed, the sufficient proof stands, and the duty ends by meeting, not by the count of voices for and against it.

What counts as sufficient proof follows from the three reasons, and the file must show which proof it is. A disinterested witness's stated taking: the witness named, no stake in the naming counting as met, no instruction from the taker about what to report, and the taking stated — the reader took the naming, not merely that it was posted where the reader might take it. An authenticated signature: the hand shown to be the reader's by exemplar, disinterested seeing, or later adoption, on a receipt identifying the naming itself. A reader's consequential act: conduct after the naming that only a met reader would show, with the conduct stated and the inference stated, needing no witness at all. In all three cases the proof goes to the meeting, not to the wording: the naming must still name the death, under T-430's content rule unchanged by escalation or by proof, and a perfectly proven delivery of a bare flag proves only that a flag was delivered, and discharges nothing, because T-430's naming rule stands.

What the insufficient proof files follows from the same rule. An interested witness's word, however detailed, files as the taker's claim — duty persisting in full, reliance still unwarned, the reader's next meeting filing exactly as it would have without any naming, unflagged unless a fresh flag is displayed, because naming warns while only display flags, under T-430's rule. A disinterested witness's account of a posting files as placement, not as meeting — the same standing a third corrected-path placement would have had, which is none. An unauthenticated signature files as a claim of acknowledgement, and a signature on a paper that does not identify the naming files as a claim about some paper, not about this naming. A taker's insistence that his witness is disinterested, with no showing of stake or instruction either way, files as a claim about the witness, not as the witness's proof. Whether disinterest is judged at the seeing or at the filing — the timing question T-433 left untouched — is admitted below as the timing-of-disinterest problem, left open.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Disinterested Witness — a witness with no stake in the naming counting as met and no instruction from the taker about what to report: FILED to T-289 — the only witness whose word is proof rather than claim. The Stated Taking — a witness's account of the reader taking the naming, not of its posting: FILED to T-289 — taking is the meeting, posting is placement. The Authenticated Signature — a signature shown to be the reader's hand, on a receipt identifying the naming: FILED to T-289 — hand plus paper, either missing, is claim. The Self-Proving Act — a reader's consequential act that proves meeting without any witness: FILED to T-289 — the act is its own witness. The Uninstructed Seeing — a seeing that counts because nothing told it what to see: FILED to T-289 — instruction is interest, even unpaid. The Interested Witness — a witness with a hand in the outcome or an instruction about what to report: VOIDED — it discharges nothing; the taker's word in another mouth is still the taker's word. The Placement Witness — a witness, however disinterested, who saw only a posting: VOIDED — it proves placement, and placement after two failures proves nothing.

**The grades.** DISINTERESTED-SEEING-SUFFICES — a disinterested witness's stated taking proves meeting; no further proof need be stacked beside it. ## T-435 — the Seeing-Time Rule *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-435 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~16:20 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-435 — the Seeing-Time Rule — designed:** T-434 left its timing-of-disinterest problem named and open: whether disinterest is judged at the seeing or at the filing — a witness disinterested when he saw the taking but interested by filing time, paid, employed, or promised in between — and whether later interest retroactively voids a proof that stood when seen, or the seeing stands as of the seeing. T-435 answers: disinterest is judged at the seeing, and the seeing stands as of the seeing. Later interest does not retroactively void a proof that stood when seen, and later disinterest does not retroactively cure a seeing taken under interest. The clock that matters is the moment the eyes were on the taking; everything after that moment is biography, not evidence about the seeing — unless the filed account itself changed after the interest attached, in which case the file no longer holds the seeing at all. A promise made at or before the seeing counts as interest at the seeing even if the payment arrives after the filing: what attaches the stake is the promise, not the payday.

The first reason is that the proof is about an event, and the event happened at the seeing. T-434 credits a disinterested witness because, at the moment of seeing, nothing pulled his account toward the outcome the taker wanted. That pull either existed then or it did not; nothing that happens afterwards can put a pull into a past moment or take one out of it. A witness paid a month after he saw the taking, for reasons that arose after the seeing and were never promised before it, saw with disinterested eyes — the money cannot travel backwards and bend the seeing. A witness who saw while holding a stake, then lost the stake before filing — the employment ended, the payment was returned, the promise was released — still saw with interested eyes, and the later loss cannot travel backwards and straighten them. The audit judges the seeing it is given, and the seeing carries the interest of its own moment, not of the filing's. To judge at the filing would make every proof hostage to the witness's later life: a proof could be voided by a hiring the witness never sought, or laundered by a resignation the taker arranged, and the taker who controls the filing date would control the proof's validity by choosing when to file.

The second reason draws the line the first reason needs, because payment timing alone would misjudge both directions. A promise is interest when made, not when kept. A witness told before the seeing, "report the taking and there will be work for you," is interested at the seeing even if the work never arrives and no coin ever changes hands — the stake attached when the words were spoken, and the seeing was taken under it. A witness told nothing before the seeing, who is offered work afterwards for reasons unrelated to the taking, is disinterested at the seeing even if he takes the work — the stake attached after the event, and the event is judged without it. The file must therefore show, for every witness, not only whether a stake exists at filing but when each stake attached: promised before the seeing, it is interest at the seeing and the proof fails; arising after the seeing, unpromised before it, it is after-acquired interest, and the proof stands. What the file may not do is read the filing-date stake backwards as if it had always been there, or read a filing-date clearance backwards as if the seeing had always been clean. Interest has a date, and the only date that counts is the seeing's.

The third reason sets the limit on both sides, because a seeing-time rule without a disclosure rule would invite concealment, and without an alteration rule would protect a doctored account. The limit on the taker's side: after-acquired interest must be filed beside the proof, not hidden. A taker who knows his witness has since taken his employment and files the witness's account as if nothing changed files a true proof inside a false file — the proof stands, but the filing is defective, and the defect must be cured by filing the later interest, after which the proof stands openly. Concealment does not void the proof, because concealment is a fault in the filing, not a fault in the seeing — but a concealed interest, once shown, reopens the question whether the filed account is still the seeing, which is the reader's opening below. The limit on the reader's side: what undoes a seeing-time proof is not the later interest itself but a showing that the account changed after the interest attached. A witness who, after becoming interested, restates, sharpens, or expands his account files a new account, not the seeing, and the audit credits only the account as it stood at the seeing — if the original account survives, in the witness's own earlier words or in a contemporaneous note, the proof stands on that; if only the restated account survives, the proof fails, not because the witness became interested but because the seeing itself can no longer be shown. Later interest alone, with the account unchanged, undoes nothing.

What counts as sufficient proof follows from the three reasons, and the file must show the dates, not merely the stakes. A seeing-time proof: the witness named, no stake and no promise at the seeing, the taking stated, and the stake history dated — every stake that attached before the seeing listed as disqualifying, every stake that attached after it listed as after-acquired and disclosed. A proof that fails at the seeing: any stake or promise attached at or before the seeing, however the witness's fortunes later changed — the seeing was taken under interest, and no later loss of the stake purifies it. A proof that stands despite later interest: a stake arising after the seeing, unpromised before it, disclosed beside the filing, with the account shown unchanged from the seeing. In all three cases the naming must still name the death, under T-430's content rule unchanged by timing or by proof, and a perfectly dated proof of a bare flag proves only that a flag was delivered, and discharges nothing, because T-430's naming rule stands.

What the insufficient proof files follows from the same rule. A witness interested at the seeing, however disinterested by filing time, files as an interested witness — duty persisting in full, reliance still unwarned, the reader's next meeting filing exactly as it would have without any naming, unflagged unless a fresh flag is displayed, because naming warns while only display flags, under T-430's rule. A witness disinterested at the seeing whose later interest is concealed files as a proof inside a defective filing — the proof stands once the interest is disclosed, but until disclosure the file is incomplete, and the taker may not rely on an undisclosed proof as if it were clean. A restated account, sharpened after interest attached with no surviving original, files as a claim about a taking, not as the taking's seeing. A taker's insistence that his witness's interest attached only after the seeing, with no dating either way, files as a claim about the calendar, not as a dated stake history. Whether disclosure of after-acquired interest must precede the filing or may supplement it afterwards — the disclosure-timing problem — and whether a restated account must be re-examined from the seeing or stands on its original words — the re-statement problem — are admitted below, left open.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Seeing-Time Rule — disinterest judged at the seeing, not at the filing, in either direction: FILED to T-289 — the seeing carries the interest of its own moment. The Promised Interest — a stake promised at or before the seeing, counting as interest at the seeing whatever the payday: FILED to T-289 — the promise, not the payment, attaches the stake. The After-Acquired Interest — a stake arising after the seeing, unpromised before it, disclosed beside the proof: FILED to T-289 — biography after the event, not evidence about it. The Filed Disclosure — the later interest stated beside the proof rather than hidden: FILED to T-289 — concealment faults the filing, not the seeing. The Unpurified Seeing — a seeing taken under interest, never cured by later loss of the stake: VOIDED — no resignation straightens eyes that saw for a stake. The Altered Account — an account restated after interest attached, with no surviving original: VOIDED — the file holds a new account, not the seeing.

**The grades.** SEEING-TIME-CONTROLS — disinterest is judged at the seeing; later interest neither voids nor later disinterest cures, in either direction. PROMISE-IS-INTEREST — a stake promised at or before the seeing is interest at the seeing, paid or unpaid. AFTER-ACQUIRED-STANDS — a stake arising after the seeing, unpromised before it, leaves the proof standing, disclosed beside it. ## T-436 — the Supplemented Disclosure *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-436 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~16:31 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-436 — the Supplemented Disclosure — designed:** T-435 left its disclosure-timing problem named and open: whether disclosure of after-acquired interest must precede the filing or may supplement it afterwards, and whether a late disclosure cures the filing defect retroactively or only from the disclosure. T-436 answers: disclosure may supplement afterwards, and the cure runs forward only. A filing is amendable — the taker who learns of his witness's later interest, or who concealed it and then corrects himself, may file the disclosure beside the proof after the fact, and the filing becomes complete from that supplement forward. But the supplement does not rewrite the window: a reader who relied on the incomplete file before the disclosure relied on an incomplete file, and that reliance stands as taken, judged by what the file then showed, not by what it shows now. The proof itself was never void — T-435 already settled that concealment faults the filing, not the seeing — so no re-proof is needed and no new witness must be found; what the disclosure cures is the filing defect, and a filing defect is cured from its cure, not from its birth.

The first reason is that a filing is a living record, not a sealed act. Filings are amended as a matter of course — a date corrected, a name spelled, a page added — and a rule that forbade supplement would force the taker to re-file the whole proof whenever a witness's fortunes changed after the filing, punishing the very cure T-435 required. T-435 orders the taker to file the later interest beside the proof; an order to file it cannot sensibly mean an order to have filed it before the filing existed, because the interest may be learned only after the filing, and a taker who concealed it may repent only after the concealment. The supplement is therefore allowed as a matter of the file's nature: the file takes additions, dates them, and stands amended. What the file may not do is pretend the addition was always there. An amendment carries its own date, and that date is part of the record — a supplement dated after the filing is a supplement dated after the filing, and any reader of the file sees both the proof and the date the interest arrived beside it.

The second reason is that the defect was in the file, not in the proof, and a cure repairs what was defective. T-435 drew that line carefully: hidden later interest defects the filing, not the proof, until disclosed. A defect in the filing is cured when the filing is completed, and a filing completed on Tuesday was incomplete on Monday — the cure runs from Tuesday forward because the file's completeness is a fact about the file at a time, and Tuesday's completeness cannot make Monday's file complete. To hold otherwise would be to let the file lie about its own past: a reader who opens the file on Wednesday would be told, in effect, that the readers of Monday saw what they never saw. The supplement therefore cures fully for the future — from the disclosure onward, the proof may be relied on openly, the filing is clean, and no reader need ask again whether the interest stands disclosed — but it cures nothing backwards. The proof's standing never needed curing, because it never fell; the filing's standing is cured from the cure; and the window between filing and disclosure remains what it was, an interval in which the file hid a stake.

The third reason is that reliance is an act in time, and acts in time are judged by what the actor could see when he acted. A reader who met the naming, trusted the witness, and acted while the interest was hidden acted on a file that hid a stake from him — he did not act on the supplemented file, because the supplemented file did not exist when he acted. The late disclosure gives him the fact late, and what he is owed after disclosure is a fresh look at his act with the fact now known — whether he may demand re-proof, or withdraw, or stand on what he did, is the reliance-window problem, admitted below, left open — but what he is not owed is a rewritten past in which his act is judged as if he had known. Conversely, a disclosure made before any reliance cures fully and without remainder: where nothing was taken on the incomplete file, there is no window to protect, and the supplemented filing stands as if the interest had been disclosed from the start — not because the supplement is retroactive, but because nothing in the interval needs its protection. The line is therefore drawn by reliance, not by the calendar alone: no reliance in the window, full cure; reliance in the window, cure forward with the reliance standing as taken.

What counts as a sufficient supplement follows from the three reasons, and the file must show the supplement, not merely the disclosure. A sufficient supplement: the later interest stated beside the proof, in the same file and on the same road the proof travelled, dated as of the supplement, reaching the same readers the proof reached — because a disclosure filed in a separate drawer, or told to different readers, is not a supplement but a second concealment, and T-431's ordinary-path rule governs the supplement's own placement exactly as it governed the naming's. A supplement filed before any reliance: the filing stands complete, the proof openly relied on from then on, the window closed with nothing in it. A supplement filed after reliance: the filing stands complete from the supplement forward, the proof openly relied on from then on, and the earlier reliance stands as reliance on an incomplete file, to be judged on its own terms. In all cases the naming must still name the death, under T-430's content rule unchanged by timing, by proof, or by supplement, and a perfectly supplemented proof of a bare flag proves only that a flag was delivered, and discharges nothing, because T-430's naming rule stands.

What the insufficient supplement files follows from the same rule. A disclosure that arrives without a date, or dated as if it had been there from the filing, files as a false record — the supplement's date is part of the supplement, and backdating it is a new concealment, not a cure. A disclosure filed apart from the proof — a side letter, a separate drawer, a telling to readers who never saw the proof — files as no supplement at all, the filing still defective, the proof still unreliably filed. A second concealment after a first disclosure — a new after-acquired interest hidden while the first stands disclosed — files as a fresh defect, restarting the defect from its own concealment, and the first disclosure cures nothing about the second. A taker's insistence that his late disclosure cures the window retroactively, so that reliance in the window counts as reliance on a complete file, files as a claim about the calendar, not as a supplemented filing. Whether a reader who relied in the window may demand re-proof, or whether the disclosure alone suffices and his act stands — the reliance-window problem — and whether a supplement must reach every reader the proof reached or only the readers who still stand to act — the supplement-reach problem — are admitted below, left open.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Supplemented Disclosure — a late disclosure filed beside the proof, allowed as an amendment, curing forward: FILED to T-289 — the file takes additions, dated as of the addition. The Forward Cure — a filing defect cured from its cure, never from its birth: FILED to T-289 — Tuesday's completeness cannot make Monday's file complete. The Unrewritten Window — the interval between filing and disclosure, standing as it was, reliance in it judged by what the file then showed: FILED to T-289 — acts in time are judged by what the actor could see. The Same-File Supplement — the disclosure sitting beside the proof, on the same road, to the same readers: FILED to T-289 — a disclosure in a separate drawer is a second concealment. The Retroactive Whitewash — a late disclosure claimed to cleanse the window backwards: VOIDED — the file may not lie about its own past. The Repeated Concealment — a new after-acquired interest hidden while an earlier one stands disclosed: FILED to T-289 — a fresh defect from its own concealment, curing nothing about the first.

**The grades.** SUPPLEMENT-IS-ALLOWED — disclosure of after-acquired interest may supplement a filing afterwards; a filing is amendable, not sealed. CURE-RUNS-FORWARD — a late disclosure cures the filing defect from the disclosure forward, never retroactively. ## T-437 — the Reliance Window *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-437 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~16:50 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-437 — the Reliance Window — designed:** T-436 left its reliance-window problem named and open: whether a reader who relied on the incomplete file before disclosure may demand re-proof, or whether the disclosure alone suffices and his act stands. T-437 answers: he may demand re-proof, and the disclosure alone does not settle his act — but the demand has a window of its own, and silence after disclosure closes it. A reader who relied in the window, on learning of the hidden interest, may demand that the taker prove the naming again, by a fresh grade. If he makes no demand, his act stands as taken, and the disclosure settles it from the disclosure forward under T-436. If he demands, the act is suspended — not undone — until the fresh proof is given or refused. If the fresh proof is given, the act stands re-grounded. If it fails or is refused, the act is unwound to the extent it can be, and the reader's next meeting files exactly as it would have without any naming.

The first reason is that reliance is the reader's act, and an act taken on a false file belongs to the actor, not to the file's later correction. T-436 settled that reliance in the window stands as taken, judged by what the file then showed — but "stands as taken" is not "stands settled." The reader acted believing the file complete; the disclosure tells him it was not. To hold that the disclosure alone settles his act would be to decide for him what his reliance was worth — the file correcting itself cannot also correct the reader's judgment, because the judgment was his, made on facts he did not have. The demand is therefore his right, not the taker's gift: only the reader who relied can say whether his reliance survives knowing the stake, and the taker who hid the stake cannot also be the one who declares the reliance cured.

The second reason is that the demand must be prompt, because a window left open forever is a second window. A reader who learns of the hidden interest and says nothing, then demands re-proof months later when the naming has become inconvenient, is not protecting his reliance — he is keeping a veto in reserve. The demand window runs from the disclosure: the reader who is told, and who continues to act on the naming without demanding, ratifies his act by continuing; the reader who demands at once holds his act suspended and the taker to his proof. The window's measure is the ordinary glance's own — the same meeting at which the disclosure is met, or the next meeting after it, and no later — because a demand made after further reliance on the supplemented file is a demand against a file the reader has already accepted. Silence after disclosure is not waiver of the proof — the proof still stands, T-435's seeing still stands — it is ratification of the act: the act stands as the reader's own, no longer as the file's.

The third reason is that the fresh proof must be a fresh grade, not the same witness re-filed. What the reliance lacked was the file's completeness: the reader trusted a file he believed complete, and it was not. Re-filing the same witness's account proves the same seeing a second time and proves nothing about completeness; the completeness question is answered only by a second, independent grade — a second disinterested witness to the taking, an authenticated hand, or a self-proving act, any grade T-434 recognizes other than the one already filed. ## T-438 — the Supplement's Reach *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-438 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~17:15 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-438 — the Supplement's Reach — designed:** T-437 left T-436's supplement-reach problem named and open: whether a supplement must reach every reader the proof reached, or only the readers who still stand to act. T-438 answers: it must reach both, but "reach" means a different thing in each direction — forward, the supplement rides attached to the proof, so every future reader meets proof and supplement together; backward, the supplement must be chased to every past reader whose reliance or standing still stands open, and to no one else. A past reader who relied on the incomplete file and has not yet ratified by silence under T-437, whose demand window still stands open, is owed the supplement in fact. A past reader who met the proof and still stands to act on the naming, though he has not yet relied, is owed the supplement on the ordinary path. A past reader whose act is already settled — ratified by silence, unwound, or lapsed beyond the demand window — is owed nothing further, and a reader who never met the proof is owed nothing as a reader, though the supplement still rides the proof wherever the proof travels next. Reach is therefore not a census of everyone the proof ever touched; it is the proof's living audience — everyone whose act the incomplete file still holds, plus everyone who may yet act on it.

The first reason is that a supplement that only rides forward abandons the readers the concealment already hurt. Attachment cures the future: no new reader need ever take an act on a file the taker knows was incomplete, because the file he meets is already supplemented. But the readers who already relied, and the readers who already stand to act, met the proof when it was bare, and a supplement filed somewhere else does not meet them. Their acts stand on the incomplete file, or their pending acts will be taken on it, unless the supplement is carried back to them. A cure that only travels forward is a cure for readers who were never harmed, and no cure at all for the readers who were. The backward chase is therefore not an extra courtesy; it is the cure itself, for the only readers a cure can help.

The second reason is that a chase to everyone the proof ever touched, including settled readers, would undo the closure T-437 bought. A reader who ratified by silence settled his act as his own; a reader whose act unwound has no act left to settle; a reader whose demand window lapsed has no demand left to make. To re-notice such a reader as if he were still owed a supplement is to hand him a second window after the first one closed — to invite a fresh demand over an act the file had already settled, and to punish the taker for a disclosure the file had already absorbed. Settled is settled: the supplement may inform a settled reader, as any filing may be read by anyone, but it is not owed to him, and his silence after a second notice opens no new window, because there is no act left for a window to hold. The chase stops where the living audience stops, or the cure becomes a second harm.

The third reason is that the standard of reaching must follow the reader's position, because reliance and standing are not the same claim on the taker. A reader who relied, with his demand window open, has an act standing on the incomplete file and a right under T-437 to demand re-proof; for him the supplement must be met in fact — the escalated standard of T-433, witnessed arrival or consequential act — because anything less leaves his window running against a notice he may never have met, and his demand right hollow. A reader who merely stands to act has no act yet standing on the file, only a future act that might be taken on it; for him placement on the ordinary path under T-431 suffices, because the supplement need only be where his next glance will find it before he acts, not proved into his hands. One standard for both would either over-prove the standing reader — demanding witnessed arrival for a man who has done nothing yet — or under-prove the relying reader, leaving his open window to run out unmet. The standard follows the stake: an act standing demands meeting in fact; an act merely pending demands only the ordinary path.

What counts as sufficient reach follows from the three reasons, and the file must show the reach, not merely the supplement. Sufficient reach: forward, the supplement filed with the proof and inseparable from it — every copy of the proof that travels after the supplement carries the supplement with it, and a copy travelling bare files as an incomplete proof, not as the proof; backward, a chase list naming every relying reader with an open window, each reached in fact, and every standing-to-act reader, each placed on the ordinary path. A supplement that reaches only some of the owed readers cures only as to those reached: as to an unreached owed reader, the filing stands exactly as it stood before disclosure — incomplete — and his T-437 demand window has not started, because it runs from his actual meeting of the supplement, not from the filing date. A failed chase, honestly made and filed at the place the proof was met, holds the backward duty open rather than discharging it: the reader's window waits for him, it does not run without him.

What the insufficient reach files follows from the same rule. A supplement filed but not attached — a separate notice lodged somewhere while the proof travels on bare — files as a second incomplete file, not as a supplemented proof, because every future reader still meets the bare proof first. A supplement chased only to the relying readers, while standing-to-act readers are left to meet the bare proof, files as a cure half-made: their future acts would be taken on a file the taker already knows is incomplete, and the taker who knew and did not place the supplement on their path owns those acts. A supplement re-noticed to a settled reader and treated as opening a fresh demand window files as a reopened settlement, not as a reach — ratification under T-437 is not undone by re-notice, and the second notice is information only. A supplement whose chase list omits an owed reader files as a cure with a hole in it: cured where it reached, incomplete where it did not, and the hole is exactly the reader it missed.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Attached Supplement — a supplement filed with the proof and inseparable from it, so every future meeting of the proof is a meeting of the supplemented proof: FILED to T-289 — the proof never travels bare again. The Chased Reader — a past reader who relied, with his demand window open, owed the supplement in fact: FILED to T-289 — his window runs from meeting, not from filing. The Standing Reader — a past reader who met the proof and still stands to act, owed the supplement on the ordinary path: FILED to T-289 — his next glance must find the supplement before he acts. The Settled Reader — a past reader whose act is ratified, unwound, or lapsed, owed nothing further: FILED to T-289 — settled is settled, and re-notice opens no new window. The Bare Proof — a copy of the proof travelling after the supplement without the supplement attached: FILED to T-289 — an incomplete proof, not the proof. The Open Window — a demand window that has not started because the supplement never reached the reader it was owed to: FILED to T-289 — a window cannot run against a man who never met what started it.

CHASE-BACKWARD-TO-THE-LIVING — the supplement is chased to every past reader whose reliance or standing still stands open, and to no one else.
