## T-439 — the Lapsed Standing *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-439 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~17:20 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-439 — the Lapsed Standing — designed:** T-438 left its standing-lapse problem named and open: whether a standing-to-act reader whose standing lapses before the supplement arrives is owed anything after lapse, or whether lapse ends the duty exactly as it ends the window. T-439 answers: lapse ends the duty, exactly and finally, while the lapse stands — but it ends only the duty of delivery, and it ends it only for the standing reader, and it never rewrites the record of what was or was not placed while he stood. A reader who still stood to act when the supplement was filed was owed the supplement on the ordinary path under T-438, because a future act of his might be taken on the incomplete file. Once his standing lapses — his deadline passes, his office ends, the act he might have taken closes without him taking it — there is no future act left for the supplement to protect, and a chase after lapse would deliver a warning to a man with nothing left to warn against. The duty dies with the standing that grounded it, as a window dies when the act it held closes. What lapse does not do is excuse a placement the taker already owed and already failed to make: if the supplement never reached the reader's ordinary path while he stood, the file must still show the gap, and the gap stands as a defect in the filing as to him, even though no delivery is owed after lapse. Delivery ends; the record does not lie.

The first reason is that T-438's duty to the standing reader was grounded in a future act, not in a past harm. The relying reader is owed meeting in fact because an act of his already stands on the incomplete file; the standing reader is owed only the ordinary path because no act of his stands yet, only an act that might be taken. Remove the might-be-taken act and nothing remains to ground the duty — no act to protect, no decision to inform, no window for the supplement to meet. A duty grounded in a pending act cannot outlive the pending act, or it would be a duty owed to a reader in the abstract, a census entry rather than a man with something at stake. Lapse is therefore not a forfeiture the reader suffers; it is the ground itself giving way. The taker who chases a lapsed standing reader is not curing anyone; he is performing a cure for an act that no longer exists.

The second reason is that lapse must be kept distinct from the two neighbouring endings, or the chain's closures collapse. A standing reader who acts on the bare proof before the supplement arrives does not lapse — he converts. His act now stands on the incomplete file, and he becomes a relying reader under T-437, with a demand window running from his meeting of the supplement and silence after that meeting ratifying his act. Conversion is not lapse: lapse is the act closing untaken, conversion is the act taken. And a reader whose act is settled by another route — ratified, unwound, or decided elsewhere — is a settled reader under T-438, owed nothing further for the same reason, but by settlement rather than by lapse. The three endings must not be confused, because they leave different records: the lapsed reader leaves a standing that closed untaken, the converted reader leaves an act standing on the file, the settled reader leaves an act already decided. Only the lapsed reader's case turns on the question T-439 answers, and its answer is that the duty ends because the act never came to be.

The third reason is that ending the duty is not erasing the gap, and the file must hold both truths at once. If the taker placed the supplement on the reader's ordinary path before lapse, the duty was discharged at placement, and lapse changes nothing — the reader's failure to read before his standing closed is his own, and no chase after lapse is owed to cure a reading he never did. If the taker failed to place it before lapse, the failure is already complete at lapse: the filing as to that reader was incomplete throughout his standing, and lapse does not retroactively cure it, any more than a supplement filed after lapse cures it. The gap stays on the record, so that any later reader of the file — an auditor, a successor, a reader whose own standing revives — can see that this reader was never placed on the path while he stood. But the gap is a record, not a live duty: it obliges no chase, opens no window, and gives the lapsed reader himself no demand after lapse, because a demand needs an act to demand about, and his act is gone. A record that both remembers the miss and refuses to chase it is not a contradiction; it is the difference between history and obligation.

What counts as a lapsed standing follows from the three reasons, and the file must show the lapse, not merely assert it. A standing lapses when the act it held closes without being taken: a deadline passes unmet, an office ends, a decision is taken by another hand so that this reader's act can no longer be taken, or the claim itself expires. The lapse must be dated in the file, because the duty's end is dated with it — a supplement placed before that date discharged the duty, a supplement placed after it is information only, and a reader whose standing is said to have lapsed on a date the file cannot show is a reader whose duty is still, for filing purposes, alive. A standing that revives — a deadline extended, an office restored, a closed act reopened — revives the duty with it, but only from the revival: the taker owes the supplement on the ordinary path from the day the reader stands again, and the revived duty does not backdate a breach, nor does it revive a gap already closed by placement before the first lapse. Revival is a new standing, not a resurrection of the old one, and the file must show the revival as its own entry, with its own date.

What lapse does not file follows from the same rule. A supplement chased to a lapsed reader and treated as opening a fresh demand window files as a reopened standing, not as a cure — lapse closed the act, and a notice after closure cannot reopen an act that no longer exists, any more than re-notice to a settled reader reopened his settlement under T-438. A reader who lapses by inaction and then claims he would have acted, had the supplement arrived, files as a wish, not as a standing — the file judges standing by acts and deadlines, not by after-the-fact claims about acts never taken, and his claim gives him no window, though it may be recorded as his own account. A supplement never placed before lapse, then filed as if placement after lapse had cured the gap, files as a false cure — the gap was complete at lapse, and a late filing cures forward for readers who still stand, never backward for a reader whose standing is gone. A standing said to have lapsed while the reader still holds an open act — a deadline not yet passed, an office not yet ended — files as a premature burial, and the duty to that reader stands until the lapse is real.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Lapsed Standing — a standing-to-act reader whose act closed untaken, deadline passed or office ended, before the supplement reached his path: FILED to T-289 — the act never came to be, and the duty died with it. The Ended Duty — a delivery duty that ends exactly when the standing that grounded it ends, while the lapse stands: FILED to T-289 — no act left, no warning owed. The Standing Gap — a record that the supplement was never placed on a lapsed reader's path while he stood: FILED to T-289 — history kept, obligation ended. The Converted Reader — a standing reader who acted on the bare proof before the supplement arrived, and thereby became a relying reader: FILED to T-289 — lapse is the act closing untaken, conversion is the act taken. The Revived Standing — a lapsed standing restored by extension, restoration, or reopening, reviving the duty from the revival date only: FILED to T-289 — a new standing, not a resurrection. The Premature Burial — a standing declared lapsed while the reader still holds an open act: FILED to T-289 — the duty stands until the lapse is real.

**The grades.** LAPSE-ENDS-DUTY — while a standing-to-act reader's standing stands lapsed, no supplement delivery is owed to him, and a chase after lapse opens no window. PLACEMENT-BEFORE-LAPSE-DISCHARGES — a supplement placed on the ordinary path before lapse discharged the duty at placement, whatever the reader then did or failed to read. ACT-CONVERTS-STANDING-TO-RELIANCE — a standing reader who acts on the bare proof becomes a relying reader under T-437, not a lapsed reader. ## T-440 — the Lapsed Reader's Claim *(audit method; design, never run)*

*T-440 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~17:35 EDT by the decoder-create-loop. Design, never run.*

**T-440 — the Lapsed Reader's Claim — designed:** T-439 left its lapsed-reader's-claim problem named and open: whether a reader who lapses by his own inaction but later claims he would have acted, had the supplement arrived, is owed a reopened window, or whether standing is judged by acts and deadlines alone and his claim is record only. T-440 answers: the claim is record only, and it reopens nothing. Standing is judged by acts and deadlines, never by a counterfactual told after the act has closed. A reader who let his deadline pass, his office end, or his act close untaken has no act for a window to hold, and a later sentence about an act he would have taken does not supply one. The file records his claim in full, in his own words, dated at the claiming — because a record that silences a lapsed reader would be a different kind of lie — but it files the claim as his account, not as his standing. It opens no window, revives no duty, backdates no breach, and erases no gap. A wish, however sincere, is not a standing; the file honours the man by writing his words down and honours the deadline by refusing to let his words move it.

The first reason is that a window needs an act, and a claim is not an act but a story about an act. T-439's lapsed reader has nothing left to warn against because the act he might have taken never came to be; T-440's claimant asks the file to pretend otherwise, to treat a sentence spoken after closure as if it were an act standing before closure. If a post-lapse claim could reopen a window, every lapse would be provisional and every deadline negotiable after the fact: any reader who missed his act could buy it back with a sentence, and no taker could ever close a file, because a claim might always arrive tomorrow to unclose it. Deadlines would cease to be deadlines and become invitations to explain oneself afterwards. The file judges standing by what was done and when — an act taken, a deadline met or missed, an office held or ended — because those are the only measures that do not move when the claimant's interests move. Sincerity does not change the measure: a claimant may be telling the exact truth about what he would have done, and still have no standing, because standing was never a measure of his inner life; it was a measure of his acts in the world before the act closed.

The second reason is that a claim must be kept distinct from the two neighbouring things it resembles, or the distinction collapses in both directions. A claim is not a pre-lapse act in progress. If the reader can show, by evidence dated before lapse, that he had already begun the act — a draft prepared, a notice of intent filed, an appointment kept toward the act — then the file is not dealing with a claim at all; it is dealing with an act, and that act is judged on its own terms, as conversion under T-437 if it stands on the bare proof, or as whatever the act itself amounts to. The claimant's later words add nothing to such an act and subtract nothing from it; the act is the evidence, and the words are commentary on it. And a claim is not a revival. A revived standing under T-439 — a deadline extended, an office restored, a closed act reopened — revives the duty from the revival date only, and a claimant's words do not effect a revival by themselves; only an actual extension, restoration, or reopening does. Confusing a claim with either neighbour either punishes a reader who really did begin his act, by reducing his act to mere words, or rewards a reader who did nothing, by promoting his words to an act. The file must hold the three apart: act, revival, and claim — the first judged by itself, the second dated at its own entry, the third recorded and nothing more.

The third reason is that recording the claim without reopening anything is not cruelty to the claimant but the only honest service the file can still do him. The claim, filed as his own account with its claim date, preserves his voice for every later reader of the file — an auditor weighing the filing, a successor holding the same office, a standing reader whose own window is still open and who may learn from the claimant's account what the supplement would have changed. What the claim may legitimately prompt is forward work for readers who still stand: a taker who hears a lapsed reader's claim and discovers the supplement was never placed at all may place it now for the readers who still stand, under T-438's forward cure, without pretending the placement cures backward for the claimant. And if the claimant later gains a genuinely new standing — a new office, a reopened act, a fresh deadline — his recorded claim informs the new standing, but the duty under that standing runs from the revival date only, under T-439, and never backdates to the lapsed act. The claim is thus neither discarded nor obeyed: it is kept where it belongs, in the record, dated at its telling, marked as a claim, so that no later reader mistakes it for a standing that was never there and no later taker mistakes silence about it for a filing that was complete.

What a claim files as follows from the three reasons, and the file must show the claim's date and its status, not merely its words. A claim told after lapse, however promptly and however plausibly, files as a Record-Only Claim: the reader's own account, dated at the claiming, filed under the lapsed standing, opening no window. A claim that arrives with pre-lapse evidence of an act begun files as an act, not as a claim, and is judged by the act — the evidence carries the weight, the words carry none. A claim treated as reopening the lapsed act, or as backdating a breach to the taker's failure to place the supplement before lapse, files as a false revival: the lapse closed the act, and a sentence cannot reopen what only an extension, restoration, or reopening can reopen. A claim dismissed without record, or recorded without its claim date, files as a silenced reader: the file has then hidden a voice it was obliged to keep, and a later auditor cannot tell whether the claim was weighed and refused or never heard at all. A claim by a reader who still stands — deadline unpassed, office unended — is not a lapsed reader's claim at all, and files under the standing reader's own rules, not under this trick.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Lapsed Reader's Claim — a reader lapsed by his own inaction who later claims he would have acted, had the supplement arrived: FILED to T-289 — a sentence after closure, not an act before it. The Record-Only Claim — a claim filed in full, in the claimant's words, dated at the claiming, opening no window and reviving no duty: FILED to T-289 — the voice kept, the deadline unmoved. The Counterfactual Standing — a standing asserted from what would have happened, rather than from what did: FILED to T-289 — judged by acts and deadlines alone, never by after-the-fact accounts. The Act in Progress — pre-lapse evidence that the reader had already begun the act, distinguished from any later claim about it: FILED to T-289 — the act is the evidence, the words are commentary. The False Revival — a claim treated as reopening a lapsed act or backdating a breach: FILED to T-289 — only an extension, restoration, or reopening revives, never a sentence. The Silenced Reader — a claim dismissed without record, or recorded without its claim date: FILED to T-289 — the file must show it weighed the claim and refused it, not that it never heard it.

**The grades.** CLAIM-IS-RECORD-ONLY — a lapsed reader's later claim that he would have acted is recorded in full and dated at the claiming, and it opens no window, revives no duty, and backdates no breach. ACTS-JUDGE-STANDING — standing is judged by acts taken and deadlines met or missed before closure, never by counterfactual accounts told after it. PRE-LAPSE-ACT-IS-NOT-CLAIM — evidence dated before lapse that the reader had begun the act is judged as an act on its own terms, and the claimant's later words add nothing to it and subtract nothing from it. CLAIM-DOES-NOT-ERASE-GAP — a claim leaves T-439's Standing Gap exactly where it was: a defect in the filing as to that reader, obliging no chase. CLAIM-MAY-PROMPT-FORWARD-WORK — a claim may prompt placement of the supplement for readers who still stand, under the forward cure, without curing backward for the claimant. CLAIM-INFORMS-NEW-STANDING-ONLY — if the claimant later gains a genuinely new standing, his recorded claim informs it, but the duty runs from the revival date only.

**T-441 — the Prompt Claim — designed:** T-440 left its claim-timeliness problem named and open: whether a claim made promptly after lapse — within days, before the taker closes the file — is treated any differently from a stale claim made months or years later, or whether promptness changes nothing because the act closed either way. T-441 answers: promptness changes nothing to the standing, and everything to the filing. A claim told the day after lapse is as record-only as a claim told years after it, because the act was closed by the lapse, not by the file's closure, and no speed of telling uncloses it. What promptness changes is where the claim sits in the record: a prompt claim files inside the still-open file before closure, so the closure record is complete when it closes; a stale claim files after closure as a supplement to a closed file, dated at its late telling, never rewriting the closure record. The prompt claimant gains a complete file, not a reopened act; the stale claimant gains a filed supplement, not a lesser record. Timeliness is a filing posture, never a standing.

The first reason is that the wrong clock is being read when promptness is measured against the file's closure. T-440's claimant asks to be judged by the calendar of the office — the file still open on his desk, the ink barely dry on the lapse — as if the act were still warm and therefore still open. But the act closed when the deadline passed, the office ended, or the act closed untaken; that is T-439's lapse, and it is the only closure that matters to standing. The taker's later closing of the file is an administrative act, the tying of the ribbon, not the closing of the act: a file can sit open for months after every act in it has closed, and a file can be closed while a standing reader's window is still running elsewhere. If promptness against file-closure could reopen anything, then standing would depend on the taker's bookkeeping speed — a slow taker would leave every lapse provisional, and a fast taker would make every lapse final by the same act that filed it. The file refuses that lottery. The claim is dated against the lapse, and every post-lapse claim, prompt or stale, stands on the same side of it: after. A claim made before the taker closes the file is still a claim made after the act closed, and the file's open cover does not make it a claim made in time.

The second reason is that promptness is not evidence, and freshness of memory must not be mistaken for an act. A prompt claimant will say, fairly, that he remembers clearly what he would have done, that the supplement's absence is still vivid, that no time has passed for his account to decay — and all of that may be true of the claim as a record. But T-440's rule turns on what the claim is, not on how well it is told: a story about an act, however fresh, is still not an act, and vividness is not a deed. The only thing that converts a post-lapse account into something more than a claim is evidence dated before lapse that the reader had already begun the act — T-440's Act in Progress — and promptness supplies none of it, because a claim told promptly after lapse is still told after lapse. To treat a prompt claim as stronger standing than a stale one would be to grade claims by their telling rather than by their acts, and to reward the claimant who speaks first over the claimant who speaks truly; the file grades neither. The prompt claim is filed in full and believed or doubted as an account on its own merits, exactly as the stale claim is; neither gains standing from the calendar of its telling, and neither loses record from it. Freshness may make the account more useful to a later auditor, and it may make forward work for standing readers faster — but usefulness is not standing, and speed is not an act.

The third reason is that promptness does change the filing, and the file must honour that difference without letting it become a standing. A prompt claim, arriving while the file is still open, files inside it: the taker writes it in, dated at the claiming, under the lapsed standing, and when the file closes, the closure record shows a claim weighed and refused — not a file that never heard one. A stale claim, arriving after closure, files as a supplement to a closed file: it is written in full, dated at its late telling, marked as post-closure, and it does not rewrite the closure record, reopen the closed acts, or backdate anything into them. In neither case does the claim hold the closure: the taker does not wait for claims before closing on schedule, and a claim arriving during closure proceedings files and the closure proceeds. What the prompt claimant truly gains is a complete closure record and the earliest possible prompt to forward work — a taker who hears promptly that a supplement was never placed may place it now for readers who still stand, under T-438's forward cure, before they too lapse, where a stale claim may arrive after those readers have lapsed as well. That is a practical gain, measured in readers still standing, not a legal gain measured in the claimant's own standing; and it is the only gain promptness buys. The stale claimant loses nothing of record for his lateness — his supplement is filed as fully as the prompt claim — and the prompt claimant gains nothing of standing for his speed.

What a claim files as follows from the three reasons, and the file must show the claim's date against the lapse, not merely against the closure. A claim told promptly after lapse, before the taker closes the file, files as a Prompt Claim: the reader's own account, dated at the claiming, filed inside the open file, opening no window and holding no closure. A claim told months or years after lapse, after the file has closed, files as a Stale Claim: the same account, dated at its late telling, filed as a post-closure supplement, rewriting nothing and reopening nothing. A claim treated as holding the file open until claims arrive, or as making closure wait on the claimant, files as a false hold: closure proceeds on schedule, and the claim files either inside the file or as its supplement. A claim treated as stronger standing because it was told promptly, or as weaker record because it was told late, files as a freshness fallacy: promptness grades neither standing nor record, and the file judges the account on its own merits in both cases. A claim filed without its date against the lapse — dated only against the closure, or undated altogether — files as a silenced reader in T-440's sense: a later auditor cannot tell whether the claim was prompt or stale, weighed before closure or supplemented after it, and the record has hidden exactly the distinction this trick exists to keep.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Prompt Claim — a claim told promptly after lapse, before the taker closes the file: FILED to T-289 — inside the open file, complete at closure, reopening nothing. The Stale Claim — a claim told months or years after lapse, after the file has closed: FILED to T-289 — a post-closure supplement, rewriting nothing, reopening nothing. The File Still Open — a file whose cover is unclosed while every act in it has already closed: FILED to T-289 — an administrative state, not a standing, and no clock for claims. The Closed-File Supplement — a claim filed after closure, dated at its late telling, marked post-closure: FILED to T-289 — the record grows, the closure stands. The Freshness Fallacy — a prompt claim treated as stronger standing, or a stale claim as weaker record, because of the calendar of its telling: FILED to T-289 — promptness grades neither standing nor record. The Unheld Closure — a closure that proceeds on schedule although a claim has arrived during closure proceedings: FILED to T-289 — the claim files, the closure is not held.

**The grades.** PROMPTNESS-CHANGES-NOTHING — a claim told promptly after lapse is as record-only as a claim told years after it; promptness changes the filing posture, never the standing. FILE-CLOSURE-IS-NOT-ACT-CLOSURE — the taker's closing of the file is administrative, and standing is measured against the lapse that closed the act, never against the file's closure. **T-442 — the Dated Telling — designed:** T-441 left its claim-dating problem named and open: whether a claim dated promptly but delivered late — written within days of lapse, received months later — counts as prompt by its writing or stale by its receipt, or whether the claim's date is its telling and the delivery delay is a filing defect of its own. T-442 answers: the claim's date is its telling, and the delay is a defect of the delivery, never of the claim. A claim written the day after lapse and carried for months before it reaches the file is a prompt claim that arrived late, not a stale claim: its telling date stands, its receipt date is written beside it, and the gap between them is charged to the carrier and to the filing, never to the claimant's posture. Promptness, under T-441, changes nothing to standing in any case — so the question is purely one of the record: and the record must show both dates, because a single date would lie about one of the two acts the claim passed through.

The first reason is that a claim is made when it is told, not when it is heard. The claimant's act is the writing — the setting down of the account, the signing of the telling, the handing of it to the road — and that act is complete at its telling whether the road is swift or slow. To date the claim at its receipt would be to let the road's speed rewrite the claimant's act: a claimant who wrote promptly and entrusted the telling to a slow carrier would stand as a stale claimant through no act of his own, and a claimant who wrote late but sent by a fast road would stand as prompt through no virtue of his own. The file refuses that lottery, just as T-441 refused the file-closure lottery. The telling date is the claim's date because the telling is the claim; the receipt is a second event, the file's meeting of the claim, and it gets its own date beside the first. A claim that arrives months after its telling files as a prompt claim with a late receipt, and any auditor reading the file sees both: told promptly, received late, and the gap named for what it is — a delay in delivery, not a delay in claiming.

The second reason is that the delay is a filing defect with an owner, and the owner is never the claimant who told promptly. The gap belongs to whoever carried the telling — the messenger, the road, the office that held it unfiled — and the cure for a filing defect is a corrected filing, not a regrading of the claim. The taker, on receiving a late-delivered prompt claim, files it dual-dated: telling date first, receipt date beside it, the gap marked as delivery delay, and the claim seated in the posture its telling earns — inside the file if the file is still open at receipt, as a supplement if the file has closed meanwhile. What the delay does not do is convert the claim: it does not make a prompt claim stale, it does not backdate a stale claim into promptness, and it does not reopen anything the lapse closed, because T-441 already settled that promptness buys no standing. The defect is cured by honesty about the dates, and the cure runs to the record, not to the claimant's standing. Where the delay was the taker's own — a telling received promptly by the office and left unfiled until after closure — the defect is T-441's unfiled-prompt-claim problem, and the same dual-dating cures it: the claim files with its true receipt date, and the closure record is supplemented, not rewritten.

The third reason is that the gap's cost falls forward, onto readers, and must be accounted there rather than charged backward onto the claimant. While the telling travelled, readers on the road may have lapsed, settled, or acted on the incomplete file — and a prompt claim that had arrived promptly might have sped T-438's forward cure to them before they lapsed, where the delayed claim arrives after they have. That loss is real, but it is the carrier's loss to answer for, not the claimant's standing to pay for: the taker owes the gap's readers what T-438 already owes them — a chase to every reader whose reliance or standing still stands open, and nothing to readers who have settled — and where the gap has closed a window that a prompt arrival would have kept open, the file says so plainly, naming the delay as the cause. The claimant's claim stays prompt in the record; the readers' loss stays charged to the delay. To charge the loss to the claimant by regrading his claim as stale would hide the carrier's failure inside the claimant's record, and the file does not launder one actor's defect through another actor's standing.

What a late-delivered claim files as follows from the three reasons, and the file must show both dates or it shows neither truly. A claim written promptly after lapse and received months later files as a Dated Telling: the account dated at its telling, the receipt date written beside it, seated in the posture its telling earns, the gap marked as delivery delay. A delay in the road, the messenger, or the office files as a Carrier's Delay: a filing defect owned by the carrier, cured by dual-dating, never by regrading the claim. A filing that shows telling date and receipt date together files as a Dual-Dated Filing: the honest form for every claim that travelled, prompt or stale. A reader who lapsed or settled during the gap files as a Gap's Reader: owed the T-438 chase if his standing still stands open, owed nothing if he has settled, and the delay named as the cause where it closed his window. A telling with no provable date — no postmark, no witness, no dated draft — files as an undated telling, dated at receipt until a telling date is proved, and the burden of proving promptness sits on the claimant who claims it. A claim backdated to a telling date it cannot prove files as a false date: the backdating is voided, the claim dates at receipt, and the backdater's account is doubted on its own merits thereafter.

UNDATED-TELLING-DATES-AT-RECEIPT — a telling with no provable date dates at receipt until a telling date is proved, and the burden of proving promptness sits on the claimant who claims it. BACKDATING-IS-VOIDED — a claim backdated to an unprovable telling date loses the backdating, dates at receipt, and its account is doubted on its own merits thereafter.

*T-442 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~18:16 EDT by the decoder-create-loop.*
**T-443 — the Self-Proved Telling — designed:** T-442 left its self-proof problem named and open: whether a telling proved only by the claimant's own word, with no postmark, witness, or draft, counts as proved at all, or whether self-proved telling dates are doubted as a class and the claim dates at receipt. T-443 answers: the telling is proved, and the date is not. The claimant's word proves that he tells — the claim exists, it is his, and it files as record under T-440 — but his word alone does not prove when he told. A self-asserted telling date files as a claimed date, marked CLAIMED beside it, and the claim's operative date is its receipt date until an outside anchor arrives. The doubt is not a judgment on this claimant's honesty; it is a rule about what one man's word can certify. His word can certify his account. It cannot certify the calendar.

The first reason is that a date is a fact about the world, not a fact about the claimant's mind. The claim's content is his to tell: what he saw, what he would have done, what he claims now — no one else can tell it for him, and his telling of it is the claim itself. The date of that telling is a different kind of fact: it sits on a calendar the claimant does not own, and it benefits him when it falls early, because an early date seats the claim inside the still-open file under T-441 and gives it the prompt posture under T-442. A rule that let a claimant certify his own early date would let every stale claim re-date itself prompt, and the distinctions T-441 and T-442 built — prompt against stale, telling against receipt — would collapse into whatever date the claimant chose to write. Self-certification of a fact that benefits the certifier is doubted as a class, not as a suspicion about one man: the file does not call him a liar, it simply refuses to let the interested party be his own calendar.

The second reason is the asymmetry between a telling now and a telling then. A telling made now is witnessed by its own receipt: the file meets it, dates the meeting, and no one need take the claimant's word that he is telling, because the telling is happening in front of the file. A telling claimed to have happened months ago leaves no such trace in the claimant's word alone, because words claiming an old date can be formed at any time and dated at will. The claimant who truly wrote the day after lapse and the claimant who writes a year later claiming he wrote the day after lapse present the file with exactly the same evidence — their word — and a rule that accepts the one must accept the other, since the file cannot tell them apart. The doubt therefore falls on the class, not the man: where the only evidence of a date is the word of the man the date would benefit, the date is unproved, whatever the truth of it. The file would rather date a truly prompt claim at its receipt than certify a single false promptness, because a false promptness corrupts the placement of every claim that follows it.

The third reason is that the doubt costs the claimant nothing he ever owned, because it touches placement, never standing or existence. Under T-440 the post-lapse claim is record-only in any case, and under T-441 promptness buys no standing, so dating an unproved claim at receipt takes no standing from the claimant — he had none to take. What the operative receipt date decides is only where the claim sits: as a supplement to a closed file rather than inside an open one, and what the T-438 chase owes the gap's readers. And the claimed date is not discarded: it files beside the receipt date, marked CLAIMED, so that corroboration can upgrade it without loss. The claimant who told promptly and can later prove it loses nothing but time; the claimant who told late and claims otherwise gains nothing but a marked claim. A rule that doubted the telling itself would silence claims; a rule that doubts only the date preserves every claim while protecting every placement.

What a self-proved telling files as follows from the three reasons, and the file must show both the claim and the doubt or it shows neither truly. A telling with no anchor beyond the claimant's word files triple-marked: the claim text filed in full as record, the claimed telling date shown beside it marked CLAIMED, and the operative date set at receipt. If an anchor arrives — a postmark, a witness to the handing, a draft bearing the date, a mention of the claim made before lapse, an office log of receipt — the claimed date is upgraded to a proved telling date, the placement is corrected forward, and the upgrade is noted as an upgrade, never silently rewritten: if the file has closed meanwhile, the closure record is supplemented with the corrected placement, never rewritten, under T-442. If an anchor contradicts the claimed date, the claimed date is struck, the operative receipt date stands, and the striking is itself filed, so no later reader meets the struck date as though it stood. A telling whose only substance is its false date — a date with no claim behind it — is voided as a dated telling; a claim with substance behind a false date files on at receipt, its text intact, its date gone.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Self-Proved Telling — a telling proved only by the claimant's own word, with no postmark, witness, or draft: FILED to T-289 — the telling stands, the date does not. The Claimed Date — a telling date asserted by the claimant alone: FILED to T-289 — shown beside the claim, marked CLAIMED, never operative until anchored. The Receipt-Dated Filing — a self-proved telling filed on its receipt date: FILED to T-289 — the operative date until an anchor arrives. The Provisional Date — a claimed date held visibly beside the receipt date while corroboration is sought: FILED to T-289 — preserved, not discarded, so an anchor can upgrade it without loss. The Anchored Date — a claimed date confirmed by an outside mark: FILED to T-289 — operative from the upgrade, noted as an upgrade, never backdated silently. The Struck Date — a claimed date contradicted by an anchor: FILED to T-289 — struck in the file, the claim re-dated at receipt, the striking itself filed. The False Date — a telling whose only substance is a date proved false: VOIDED to T-289 — voided as a dated telling, its text, if any, filing undated at receipt as record.

**T-444 — the Corroboration Threshold — designed:** T-443 left its corroboration-threshold problem named and open: whether a single witness, a draft fragment, a mention made before lapse, or an office log suffices as an anchor for a telling date, or whether some anchors need a second mark beside them, and whether a prior mention counts when the mention itself is proved only by the claimant's word. T-444 answers: the threshold is independence plus fixation, not count. A single outside mark suffices when it is both independent of the claimant and fixed at the time it purports to mark; a mark that fails either test needs a second mark beside it, and a mention proved only by the claimant's word is not a mark at all. One disinterested witness to the handing suffices alone. One ordinary-course record — a postmark, a carrier's log, an office log made in the ordinary run of business — suffices alone. A bare draft fragment does not: it proves the words existed, not when they were set down, and it needs a second mark — a lodging, a postmark, a dated mention in an outside record — before it dates anything. An interested witness needs a second mark too. And a prior mention counts only when the mention itself is anchored outside the claimant's word; a mention that exists only because the claimant says it does is self-proof wearing a second coat, and it anchors nothing.

The first reason is that a date needs a mark the claimant cannot move after the fact. A postmark is fixed by another's machine at the moment of posting; a carrier's log is fixed by another's hand in the ordinary course; a disinterested witness's memory is fixed in another mind, one with nothing to gain from the date it carries. A draft in the claimant's own drawer has none of that fixity: it can be written, rewritten, and backdated at leisure, and nothing in the paper itself says which day it was written on. The question is never how many marks there are but whether any mark stands where the claimant's hand cannot reach it after the telling. A single mark in such a place proves the date; a shelf of marks all within his reach proves only that he keeps a shelf.

The second reason is that counting marks instead of weighing them fails in both directions. It under-counts the strong single anchor: one disinterested witness who saw the handing proves the telling date as surely as any crowd, and demanding a second witness for a date already proved would delay every upgrade for no gain in certainty. And it over-counts the weak many: three repetitions of the claimant's own story, or a draft plus a mention both drawn from his own papers, are one source counted three times, not three sources. The threshold must therefore be about source, not tally. Two weak anchors can combine into one sufficient anchor, but only when they fix the same date from different sides — an undated draft plus a dated log of its lodging, for example — so that the pair together supplies both the words and the day. Two marks from the same hand, the same drawer, or the same telling count as one mark, however many pieces they arrive in.

The third reason is that recursion must stop somewhere, or T-443's rule is empty. If a prior mention proved only by the claimant's word could anchor his claimed date, then every claimed date would arrive with its own prior mention attached, and self-proof would bootstrap itself into proof: the claimant would need only to say "I mentioned it before" to convert every CLAIMED date into a proved one. The file must refuse that circle. A mention anchors a date only when the mention itself can be shown without the claimant's help — a letter received by another, an entry in another's diary, a log line written by another's hand. Where the mention's only witness is the claimant, the mention and the claim stand or fall together, and together they are still one man's word. The threshold is not a suspicion of this claimant; it is the shape of proof itself, which must somewhere touch ground outside the man it benefits.

What a threshold-met telling files as follows from the three reasons. When the threshold is met, the claimed date upgrades under T-443: the date becomes operative from the upgrade, the upgrade is noted as an upgrade, and the placement is corrected forward, never silently rewritten. When the threshold is not met, the telling stays triple-marked under T-443: claim text in full as record, claimed date beside it marked CLAIMED, operative date at receipt. A pair of weak anchors that together meet the threshold files as a Paired Anchor, with both marks named in the file, so a later reader can see that the date rests on the pair and on neither piece alone. If an anchor later fails — a witness recants, a log is shown misdated, a postmark proved forged — the date is struck, the operative receipt date stands again, and the striking is itself filed, exactly as a contradicted date is struck under T-443; the failure of one anchor does not by itself void the claim, which files on at receipt with its text intact.

**T-445 — the Separate Roofs — designed:** T-444 left its independence-boundary problem named and open: whether two weak anchors from the same household, office, or circle count as independent, or whether independence requires separate roofs, separate routines, or separate interests. T-445 answers: independence is separate seeings, not separate roofs. Two anchors are independent when neither learned the date from the other, from the claimant, or from a common telling — when each fixes the date from its own seeing, at its own time, through its own channel. A shared roof, office, or circle does not by itself merge two anchors, and separate roofs do not by themselves split them. The test is a counterfactual: would the second anchor still fix the same date if the first had never existed and the claimant had never spoken? If yes, the anchors are two. If the second's date traces to the first, to the claimant, or to a telling both drank from, the file holds one anchor reported twice, and the pair counts once until a third outside mark arrives.

The first reason is that proof must touch ground in two places, not one place twice. A household that heard the telling together gives the file one seeing reported by two mouths: husband and wife who sat in the same room while the claimant told his claim on the same evening did not each witness the date — they witnessed one telling, and their two accounts are one account in stereo. Counting them as two would let a single telling bootstrap itself into a threshold-met date, the same circle T-444 refused when it barred a self-proved mention from anchoring a self-proved date. The file does not doubt either witness; it refuses to double-count a single seeing. Conversely, two housemates who saw separately — one who watched the handing at the door in the morning, one who met the claim on the road that evening, neither having conferred with the other — give the file two seeings under one roof, and the roof is no reason to merge them. What the file counts is seeings, and a roof is neither a seeing nor a merger of seeings.

The second reason is that roofs are a proxy, and proxies misfire in both directions. Separate roofs can hide a single source: two friends in different towns, each told the date by the claimant over the same telephone week, are one telling wearing two addresses, and a rule that counted roofs would certify them as independent while the claimant laughed. One roof can hold two genuine seeings: a clerk who logged the receipt in the morning routine and a carrier who postmarked the parcel that afternoon work under one office roof but through separate routines, and neither took the date from the other. A rule that merged by roof would discard a true pair; a rule that split by roof would certify a false one. The file must therefore judge the chain of knowledge — who learned the date from whom, by what channel, at what time — and not the address on the envelope. The roof is evidence about the chain, never a substitute for it: shared walls raise the question, they do not answer it.

The third reason is that interest, not address, is what truly merges anchors. What makes two marks one mark is a shared benefit from the date falling early, or a shared telling that fixed the date for both. Members of one family, firm, or cause who share the benefit count as one interest until each shows a separate seeing and no stake of his own — not because they share a roof, but because the date pays them alike. A disinterested housemate who saw separately, with nothing to gain from the date, is worth more to the file than two interested strangers in different counties who were both told the date by the claimant. And interest is judged by the benefit, not the blood: a stranger who stands to gain from the early date is merged with the claimant's interest, while a kinsman who stands to lose nothing and gains nothing, and who saw for himself, stands alone. The merge rule is therefore: same benefit or same telling, one anchor; separate seeings and separate stakes, two — whatever the roofs.

What a boundary-tested pair files as follows from the three reasons, and the burden sits where it belongs. A pair whose separateness is shown — each anchor named with its seeing: its time, its place, its channel, and the absence of conferring between the makers — files as Separate Seeings and counts twice, meeting T-444's threshold as a Paired Anchor. A pair whose separateness is not shown — two marks from one household, office, or circle with no account of separate seeings — files as a Single-Source Pair: both marks named in the file, counting once, needing a third outside mark before the date upgrades under T-443. The claimant bears showing separateness, because he is the man the early date would benefit, and the file does not presume what benefits him. Where the file cannot tell whether the makers conferred, doubt resolves against independence: the pair counts once, and the doubt is itself filed, so a later reader can see that the date rests on one counted anchor and one waiting mark, not on two. A pair later shown to share a telling — one maker found to have learned the date from the other — is re-filed from Separate Seeings down to a Single-Source Pair, and any placement upgraded on the pair is corrected forward under T-444's Failed Anchor rule, never silently rewritten.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Separate Roofs — the test of whether two anchors are independent: FILED to T-289 — independence is separate seeings, not separate addresses. The Single Seeing — two reports of one hearing, one telling, one handing: FILED to T-289 — counts once, however many mouths report it. The Separate Seeings — two seeings at different times, places, or channels, without conferring between the makers: FILED to T-289 — count twice, and meet the threshold as a pair. *T-445 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~19:03 EDT by the decoder-create-loop.*

**T-446 — the Untouched Date — designed:** T-445 left its conferring problem named and open: whether witnesses who saw separately but talked before telling lose independence, or whether only conferring about the date itself merges them, or only conferring that changes a date does. T-446 answers: talk merges only when it carries the date. Conferring that never touches the date leaves independence standing: two witnesses who saw separately and talked about the road, the weather, or the claim's substance without its date still give the file two seeings, and their talk is filed, not punished. Conferring that touches the date but changes nothing — each witness arrived at the talk already holding the same date and left holding it still — also leaves independence standing, but only when the pre-talk possession is shown by a mark outside the witnesses' post-talk word: a prior note, a prior telling to a third party, an ordinary-course record made before the talk. Conferring that touches the date and changes nothing, with no such pre-talk mark, counts once: the witnesses' word that they already held the date is the very thing the talk could have supplied, and the file does not take it on trust. And conferring that supplies a date to a witness who had none, or changes a witness's date to another's, merges the pair outright: the resulting date is the talk's date, not a seeing's date, and it counts once until a third outside mark arrives.

The first reason is that T-445 counts the chain of knowledge, not the conversation. What makes two marks two is that each date came from its own seeing, and talk is a channel like any other: a channel that carried no date carries no contamination. Two men who met on the road and talked about the claimant's character, the state of the road, or the claim itself without ever naming a day did not exchange dates, and to merge their seeings for having spoken would punish ordinary human contact while leaving the real contamination — a date passed from mouth to mouth — untouched. The file must therefore ask, of every talk between witnesses, the same question it asks of every channel: did this carry the date? A talk that carried nothing but company leaves the counterfactual intact — each witness would still fix the same date with the other erased — and a pair that passes the counterfactual is two, whatever was said between the seeings.

The second reason is that confirmation without a pre-talk mark is self-proof wearing a second coat. A witness who says "I already knew the date before we talked" asks the file to believe, on his word alone, the very fact that would rescue his independence — and T-443 already refused exactly that move when it barred a claimant's word from proving his own date. If post-talk assurance sufficed, every merged pair could be laundered into a separate pair by the simple expedient of both witnesses agreeing, after the talk, that they had always agreed. The pre-talk mark is therefore not pedantry but the only thing standing between the confirmation rule and its own abuse: a note predating the talk, a telling to a third party predating the talk, a record made in the ordinary course predating the talk. Where such a mark exists, the confirmation is proved from outside the talk, and the pair stands. Where it does not, the pair counts once, and the doubt is filed — not as a finding that the witnesses conferred about the date, but as a finding that the file cannot tell whether they did, which under T-445 resolves against independence.

The third reason is that a supplied or changed date belongs to the talk, not to the seeing. A witness who arrived dateless and left dated reports the conversation, not his eyes; a witness who arrived holding one date and left holding another reports the conversation's revision of his eyes. Counting either as a second seeing would double-count the talker: the first witness's date, reported once by its seer and once by its hearer, would pass T-444's threshold on a single source. The displaced date, where one existed, must still be filed — as a Superseded Seeing, named with its original date and the talk that displaced it — never silently erased, because a later reader who finds the change must be able to see that a change happened, and in which direction. A merged pair is not a disgraced pair: both marks stay named in the file, counting once, needing a third outside mark before the date upgrades, exactly as T-445's Single-Source Pair requires.

What a talked pair files as follows from the three reasons, and the burden sits where it belongs. A pair whose talk is named — who talked, when, and about what — and whose talk never touched the date files as Conferring Noted and counts twice. A pair whose talk touched the date but changed nothing, with a pre-talk mark for each witness's prior possession, files as a Confirmed Date and counts twice. A pair whose talk touched the date but changed nothing, with no pre-talk mark, files as a Single-Source Pair: both marks named, counting once, until a pre-talk mark or a third outside mark arrives. A pair whose talk supplied or changed a date files as a Talked Date: both marks named, counting once, the supplied or changed date marked as the talk's, the displaced date filed as a Superseded Seeing. The claimant bears showing pre-talk possession, because he is the man the early date would benefit. Talk discovered later — a conversation the file did not know of when the pair was counted twice — re-files the pair downward at once, and any placement upgraded on the pair is corrected forward under T-444's Failed Anchor rule, never silently rewritten.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Untouched Date — the test of whether talk between witnesses breaks independence: FILED to T-289 — talk merges only when it carries the date. The Conferring Noted — talk between witnesses that never touched the date: FILED to T-289 — filed, not punished, the pair counting twice. The Confirmed Date — a date each witness held before the talk and holds still after it: FILED to T-289 — counts twice only with a pre-talk mark for each. The Pre-Talk Mark — a note, a prior telling to a third party, or an ordinary-course record predating the talk: FILED to T-289 — the outside proof that confirmation is not self-proof. The Talked Date — a date supplied or changed by talk: FILED to T-289 — the talk's date, not a seeing's, counting once. The Superseded Seeing — a date displaced by talk: FILED to T-289 — filed, never erased, named with the talk that displaced it. The Unshown Pre-Talk Possession — a confirmation claimed without a pre-talk mark: FILED to T-289 — doubt resolved against independence, the pair counting once, the doubt filed. The Date-Carrying Talk — any talk that names, supplies, or revises a date: FILED to T-289 — the only kind of talk that merges.

**The grades.** TALK-MERGES-ONLY-WHEN-IT-CARRIES-THE-DATE — conferring that never touches the date leaves two seeings two. CONFIRMATION-NEEDS-A-PRE-TALK-MARK — a date held before the talk counts only when a mark outside the witnesses' post-talk word proves it. POST-TALK-ASSURANCE-IS-SELF-PROOF — a witness's word that he already held the date is the thing the talk could have supplied, and the file does not take it on trust. SUPPLIED-DATE-IS-THE-TALK'S-DATE — a witness who arrived dateless and left dated reports the conversation, not his eyes. CLAIMANT-SHOWS-PRE-TALK-POSSESSION — the man the early date would benefit bears showing that confirmation predates the talk. *T-446 trick seeded 2026-10-24 ~19:17 EDT by the decoder-create-loop.*

**T-447 — the Rehabilitated Date — designed:** T-446 left its rehabilitation problem named and open: whether a witness whose date was supplied or changed by talk, and whose talked date is later backed by a third outside mark, is rehabilitated into a second seeing, or whether the talked date stays the talk's forever and only the third mark counts. T-447 answers: the date is rehabilitated; the witness is not. A talked date backed by a third outside mark — a mark independent of the talker, the talked witness, and the talk itself — stands as anchored: the talker's seeing plus the third mark meet T-444's threshold, and the date upgrades. But the talked witness does not become a second seeing: his report stays a Standing Echo, named in the file and counting nothing. If the third mark later fails, the date falls back to the talker's single anchor, not to two, because the echo never held weight of its own. The witness himself is rehabilitated only by his own evidence — a pre-talk mark found later, proving he held the date before the talk, which converts the Talked Date into a Confirmed Date under T-446. Truth of the date and independence of the witness are different questions, and different marks answer them.

The first reason is that T-444's threshold counts anchors, not biographies. What a date needs is two independent marks fixing it, and a third mark independent of the talker supplies the second leg the talked pair lacked. The talked witness's report adds nothing to that count, but it subtracts nothing either: the date no longer leans on him at all. To refuse the upgrade because one of the three reports in the file is tainted would punish the date for company it no longer needs, and would leave a date fixed by two independent seeings standing as unanchored for the sake of a witness who is no longer load-bearing. The file judges the date by its anchors, and the talker's anchor plus the third mark's anchor are two anchors, whatever the echo says beside them.

The second reason is that borrowed independence is no independence at all. A witness rehabilitated by another's mark would be a witness whose independence was lent to him, and T-445's counterfactual forbids exactly that loan: erase the third mark and ask whether the talked witness would still fix the date — he would not, because his date came from the talk, and the talk is still the talk however many other marks now agree with it. That is why the talked witness files as a Standing Echo rather than a second seeing: named, because the file never erases a report, and counting nothing, because a report that traces to the talk traces to one source. If the third mark fails — recants, shown misdated — the date re-files downward under T-444's Failed Anchor rule to the talker's single anchor, and the echo stays an echo; the file does not discover, on the third mark's failure, that it had two seeings all along, because it never did.

The third reason is that the witness has his own road back, and it runs through his own past, not through the date's present. A pre-talk mark found later — his own note predating the talk, a telling to a third party predating the talk, an ordinary-course record predating the talk — proves he held the date before the talk, and under T-446 that converts the Talked Date into a Confirmed Date: two seeings, the pair counting twice. The third mark about the date cannot do this work, because it proves the date is true, not that the witness knew it independently; and the pre-talk mark cannot do the third mark's work, because it proves the witness knew the date, not that the date is the right one. The file therefore keeps two rehabilitations apart: the date's rehabilitation, by an independent third mark, which upgrades the date's standing; and the witness's rehabilitation, by his own pre-talk mark, which upgrades the pair's count. Either alone suffices for its own question; neither answers the other's.

What a talked date backed by a third mark files as follows from the three reasons, and the burden sits where it belongs. A talked date with a third outside mark independent of the talker, the talked witness, and the talk files as a Rehabilitated Date: the date counts as anchored, the talked witness's report files as a Standing Echo, named and counting nothing. A third mark that drank from the talk — the go-between's own note, the shared letter, a record both witnesses consulted — is not a third mark at all: it is the talk in a third hand, and the date stays a Talked Date counting once. A third mark that later fails re-files the date downward to a Talked Date under T-444's Failed Anchor rule, corrected forward, never silently. A pre-talk mark for the talked witness found later re-files the pair upward to a Confirmed Date under T-446, the witness rehabilitated by his own past. The claimant bears showing the third mark's independence from the talk, because he is the man the upgraded date would benefit, and doubt about the third mark's independence resolves against the upgrade, exactly as T-445 resolves doubt against independence.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Rehabilitated Date — a talked date backed by an independent third mark: FILED to T-289 — the date counts as anchored, the witness staying an echo. The Standing Echo — a talked witness's report beside a rehabilitated date: FILED to T-289 — named, counting nothing, neither struck nor counted. The Borrowed Independence — independence lent to a witness by another's mark: FILED to T-289 — refused, the counterfactual forbids it. The Date's Rehabilitation — the upgrading of a date's standing by a third mark: FILED to T-289 — answers whether the date stands, not whether the witness saw. The Witness's Rehabilitation — the upgrading of a witness's count by his own pre-talk mark: FILED to T-289 — answers whether the witness saw, not whether the date stands. The Third Mark's Independence — the requirement that the third mark drink from neither the talker, the talked witness, nor the talk: FILED to T-289 — a mark that drank from the talk is the talk in a third hand. The Failed Third Mark — a third mark that later fails: FILED to T-289 — the date re-files down to a Talked Date, the echo staying an echo. The Two Rehabilitations — the date's and the witness's, kept apart: FILED to T-289 — either alone suffices for its own question, neither answers the other's.

**The grades.** DATE-REHABILITATED-WITNESS-NOT — a third mark upgrades the date's standing and leaves the talked witness an echo. THIRD-MARK-ANCHORS-THE-DATE — the talker's seeing plus an independent third mark meet T-444's threshold. BORROWED-INDEPENDENCE-IS-NONE — a witness whose independence comes from another's mark has none, by the counterfactual. ECHO-COUNTS-NOTHING-STAYS-NAMED — a talked report beside a rehabilitated date is named and counts for nothing. THIRD-MARK-FAILURE-REVERTS — a failed third mark drops the date back to a Talked Date, corrected forward. PRE-TALK-MARK-REHABILITATES-THE-WITNESS — only the witness's own pre-talk evidence converts an echo into a seeing. TRUTH-AND-INDEPENDENCE-ARE-DIFFERENT-QUESTIONS — the third mark answers whether the date stands, the pre-talk mark answers whether the witness saw. **T-448 — the Echo's Reader — designed:** T-447 left its echo-reliance problem named and open: whether a Standing Echo that later readers rely on — a reader who dates from the echo, not knowing it was an echo — creates any reliance the file must correct, or whether the echo's naming in the file discharges the duty. A Standing Echo named in the file carries its warning with it, and a reader who reads the file reads the warning — for that reader the file has done its duty, and no chase is owed. But an echo that travels — a reprint, a stripped copy, an oral retelling, any form T-438 already knows travels without its file — carries no warning, and a reader who dates from that detached echo dates from what looks like a second seeing. That reader's reliance is real whether or not the file named the echo, because the naming never reached him. The file therefore owes him an Echo Correction: a notice, sent to the place his placement was made, that the leg he stood on was an echo, naming the third mark the date actually stands on.

The first reason is that notice is notice only to those it reaches. A warning written in a file warns the file's readers; it warns nobody who never opened the file. T-447's naming rule, read as discharging the duty outright, would treat a warning nobody saw as a warning everybody heard, and a duty discharged by ink nobody read is no discharge at all. The duty follows the echo's travel, not the echo's label: wherever the echo went without its warning, the correction must go after it.

The second reason is that reliance is a fact about the reader's placement, not about the echo's label. The duty is not owed to everyone who could have relied — a reader who merely saw the echo, or who dated from other marks, is owed nothing, and the file chases no ghosts. It is owed to the reader who shows reliance: his own placement citing the echo as a leg, his own date resting on it. Shown reliance, not presumed reliance, is what converts a named echo into an owed correction, and the burden of showing it sits on the reader who claims it, just as T-445 put the burden of showing separateness on the man the early date would benefit.

The third reason is that the correction is surgical: it strikes the leg, not the date. The Rehabilitated Date never stood on the echo — it stood on the talker's seeing plus the third mark — so telling the reader his leg was an echo does not un-anchor his date. If his placement can be re-anchored on the third mark, it files as a Re-anchored Date and stands; if his placement cited only the echo and no other leg, the date falls with the leg, and that fall is the correction's honest work, not its overreach. A correction that un-anchored the whole date would punish the reader for the file's own travelling echo; a correction that left the leg standing would leave the next reader to date from it again.

**T-449 — the Chained Echo — designed:** T-448 left its chained-echo problem named and open: whether an Echo's Reader whose echo was itself a reprint of a reprint — an echo passed hand to hand, each hand further from the file — is owed a chase through every hand, or only to the reader the file can find, and whether an unfound reader's reliance simply stands uncorrected. T-449 answers: only to the reader the file can find, and directly — never through the chain. The file owes a correction to each findable reader who placed a date on a chained echo, sent straight to his placement, not relayed hand to hand through the intermediaries who carried it. A hand that merely carried the echo and placed nothing on it is owed nothing and carries nothing: the chase does not stop at his door, because it never started there. And a reader the file cannot find is not chased through ghosts — his reliance stands uncorrected, filed as an Unfound Reliance, and the file carries a Standing Correction beside the echo, waiting for the day he reappears on the road.

The first reason is that a chain is not a road. A road is the file's own readers, each met in the file or at a placement the file can name; a chain is a succession of private hands, each further from the file than the last, and the file cannot know how many hands there were, let alone where the last one stands. A duty to chase through every hand would be a duty to chase an unknown number of unknown people to unknown places — a duty that can never be shown discharged, and therefore a duty that can never be kept. T-448 already refused to chase ghosts for mere sight of an echo; T-449 refuses the same ghosts one hand further out, because a hand that placed nothing shows no reliance to correct, and a hand that did place a date is not a relay but a reader in his own right, owed his own correction directly.

The second reason is that relay corrupts the correction. A correction passed hand to hand arrives, if it arrives at all, as a retelling of a retelling — the same travel that stripped the echo of its warning in the first place, now stripping the correction of its precision. The Echo Correction T-448 designed names the third mark the date stands on; relayed through hands that never saw the file, that name degrades into a rumour that a date was wrong somewhere, and a rumour is not a correction. A direct correction to the placement preserves the name; a chained correction preserves only the alarm. The file therefore sends one correction per placement, to the placement, and never asks a carrier to carry it onward.

The third reason is that an unfound reliance standing uncorrected is not a reliance validated. Standing uncorrected means exactly what it says: no correction has reached it, so it stands as it was placed — on an echo, counting nothing as a second seeing — and any reader who later meets that placement meets it with the file's Standing Correction beside the echo, if he meets it in the file at all. The file does not bless the placement by failing to find its reader, and it does not strike the placement for a failure that was the file's, not the reader's. The debt is recorded, not discharged: when the unfound reader reappears — a new filing, a new placement, a re-meeting on the road — the Standing Correction applies to him then, as if the chase had found him at last.

What a chained echo files as follows from the three reasons, and the burden sits where it belongs. A reader whose placement the file can locate, however many hands the echo passed through to reach him, files as a Findable Reader: owed one Echo Correction directly to his placement, exactly as T-448's Echo's Reader was owed, the length of the chain changing nothing about the correction and nothing about the date. A hand that carried the echo onward without placing a date on it files as nothing at all: no correction owed, no relay duty imposed, no standing gained by carrying. A reader whose placement the file cannot locate files as an Unfound Reliance: his date stands uncorrected and unvalidated, and the file's Standing Correction waits beside the echo for his reappearance, applying on re-meeting without reopening anything his absence closed.

**T-450 — the Carried Warning — designed:** T-449 left its warning-travel problem named and open: whether a hand who reprints the echo with its warning attached — a carrier who passes the naming along with the echo — discharges the readers downstream of him, or whether only the file's own naming counts and a carrier's warning is hearsay of a warning. T-450 answers: neither extreme, and the middle is the rule — the carried warning warns, but it does not discharge. A downstream reader who receives the echo with its warning attached is put on notice, and he cannot afterwards plead that he placed his date in innocence of the echo; but the file's own correction duty is not discharged by the carrier's act, because a carrier's warning is notice of a naming, not the naming itself, and only the file's naming carries the remedy the reader is owed.

The first reason is that notice and naming are different acts, and only one of them can be carried. A warning says: this date rests on an echo, and an echo counts nothing as a second seeing. That is a statement about the leg, and a carrier can carry it faithfully — he need only copy the warning with the echo. A naming says: this echo, this date, and this third mark the date stands on instead. That is a statement about the remedy, and a carrier cannot carry it, because he never saw the file and never saw the third mark; at best he carries a report that such a mark exists somewhere, which is a rumour of a remedy, not a remedy. The downstream reader is therefore warned and unremedied at once: he knows his leg is an echo, and he does not know what leg would hold his date instead. A warning that cannot name the replacement cannot discharge the duty to name it.

The second reason is that a carrier's warning is hearsay in exactly the sense T-449 feared, and hearsay cannot discharge a duty that exists to be verifiable. The file's own naming is verifiable in the file: a reader who meets it there can check the echo, the date, and the third mark together, and can see whether the naming still stands or has since been withdrawn. A carrier's warning is verifiable nowhere: the downstream reader cannot check, from the carrier's copy, whether the file really named this echo, in these words, or whether the naming was later withdrawn, or whether the carrier invented the warning, garbled it, or attached another file's warning to this echo by mistake. The file does not discharge a verifiable duty by accepting an unverifiable report that the duty was done. When the file finds the reader, it still owes him its own Echo Correction, directly to his placement, exactly as T-449 ordered — the carried warning changes nothing about the correction's route, its addressee, or its content.

The third reason is that what the carried warning does change is the reader's posture, not the file's duty — and the posture change is real enough to file. A reader who receives the echo with its warning attached and places a date on it anyway files as a Warned Reader, and his placement files as a Knowing Reliance: a date placed knowing the leg is an echo. A Knowing Reliance counts nothing — the warning is not a mark, not an anchor, and not a seeing, and it proves nothing about the date, only about the reader's knowledge — but it differs from a blind reliance in one filed respect: the Warned Reader cannot later claim his date was innocently placed, and cannot ask to be treated as a reader the file failed to warn. He was warned; the warning simply was not the file's. And a hand who reprints the echo without its warning restores the downstream reader to blindness: a reader downstream of a stripping stands as unwarned, and the stripping is filed as the stripper's act, never as the reader's fault — a reader cannot lose innocence he was never given.

What a carried warning files as follows from the three reasons, and the burden sits where it belongs. A reader who received the echo with a faithful warning attached files as a Warned Reader: owed the file's own Echo Correction still, when found, but barred from pleading innocent reliance, his placement a Knowing Reliance counting nothing. A carrier who passes the warning along files as a carrier only: he has warned, he has not named, he has discharged nothing, and he bears no duty to carry the correction onward — T-449 already refused him that relay. A warning that names the defect — that the date rests on an echo counting nothing as a second seeing — files as a Carried Warning; a vague label that warns of something without naming echo-ness, such as a bare "unverified" tag, files as a Partial Warning: it puts the reader on inquiry, but it does not make him a Warned Reader, because a reader put on inquiry about everything has been warned about nothing in particular.
