**T-451 — the Garbled Warning — designed:** T-450 left its warning-fidelity problem named and open: whether a carried warning that arrives garbled, partial, or altered in transit still warns, or whether any infidelity voids the warning and restores the downstream reader to innocence. T-451 answers: fidelity is graded, not binary — a warning that keeps its core still warns however garbled its wording, and a warning that loses its core warns nothing, however faithfully its shell was copied. The core is one sentence: this leg is an echo, and an echo counts nothing as a second seeing. A carried warning that preserves that sentence, in any words, puts the downstream reader on notice under T-450, and he cannot afterwards plead innocence of the echo. A carried warning that drops that sentence, reverses it, or attaches it to the wrong echo is not a degraded warning but no warning at all — and a reversed or misattached warning is worse than silence, because it does not merely leave the reader unwarned, it actively certifies a leg the file has already condemned.

The first reason is that a warning warns by its content, not by its pedigree. T-450 already separated notice from naming: the carrier cannot carry the remedy, but he can carry the doubt. Doubt travels in the sentence that names it, and a sentence survives rewording, abbreviation, and even clumsy copying so long as the doubt it names survives with it. A warning copied with a dropped adjective, a transposed clause, or a carrier's own plain-words paraphrase still says the leg is an echo, and a reader who reads it knows what he is standing on. To void such a warning for infidelity of wording would be to demand that doubt arrive in the file's exact words or not at all — which is to demand the file's naming under another name, and T-450 refused exactly that demand. The test, therefore, is the core, not the copy: does the downstream reader, reading what actually arrived, learn that his leg is an echo? If yes, he is a Warned Reader, and the carrier's garble is a blemish on the road, not a pardon for the reader.

The second reason is that the core test cuts the other way with equal force, and the file must not pretend otherwise. A warning that arrives saying the echo is confirmed, that the second seeing has been supplied, or that the doubt has been cleared reverses the core, and a reversed warning does not warn badly — it un-warns. The reader who trusts it places his date with a confidence the file never gave him, and his confidence is the carrier's work, not his own innocence. Likewise a warning attached to the wrong echo — the right doubt, the wrong leg — warns nobody about the leg it lands on, and leaves the leg it belongs to unwarned; misattachment is not partial fidelity but a filing error with a victim at each end. In both cases the reader is not a Warned Reader at all: he was told the opposite of the truth, or told the truth about something else. The file records him as unwarned, and the blame for his unwarned state is assigned, not absorbed: the carrier bears the garble he introduced, whether by copying error, paraphrase drift, or misattachment, and the file's own correction duty under T-450 stands entirely undischarged until its own naming arrives. A garbled warning never discharges the file, because discharge was never the carrier's to give; it only ever warned, and where it failed to warn, it failed completely.

The third reason is that grading fidelity protects both ends of the road from the two frauds a binary rule would invite. A binary rule that any garble voids the warning would let every Warned Reader plead a dropped comma back into innocence, and no carrier's warning would ever stick — the downstream reader could always find a blemish and claim he never knew. A binary rule that any warning-shaped arrival warns would let a carrier's reversed or misattached copy certify condemned legs wholesale, and the file would have to honour warnings that lie. The graded rule admits neither fraud: the reader cannot plead a blemish against a core he plainly read, and the carrier cannot plead a shell against a core he plainly lost. Between the two poles lies the honest middle the file already keeps for other partial things — T-450's Partial Warning, which is inquiry only, is the sibling here: a warning that keeps the core but loses its date, its source, or its scope still warns, and still owes the reader the file's naming; it does not warn less, it warns without the particulars, and the particulars are the file's to supply, never the carrier's to invent.

**T-452 — the Distrusted Carrier — designed:** T-450 left its warning-source problem named and open: whether a warning from a hand the reader had reason to distrust still warns — whether notice depends on the carrier's credit, or whether a warning warns whoever reads it regardless of who carried it. T-452 answers: the warning warns whoever reads it, regardless of the carrier. Notice is a property of the content read, never of the hand that carried it. A reader who reads the sentence "this leg is an echo" knows the doubt it names whether the sentence arrived from a trusted clerk or a known liar, and he cannot afterwards plead that he never knew what he plainly read. The carrier's credit belongs to the carrier's account, not to the reader's state; it may decide whether the reader believes the warning, but belief is not the test — notice is.

The first reason is that knowledge once read is not unread by distrust. Distrust may make a reader verify, discount, or investigate, but none of those acts un-reads the sentence. A reader who distrusts his carrier and places anyway places with the doubt in front of him; he may doubt the warning's truth, but doubting a warning is itself notice that the leg is contested, and a contested leg placed upon is a placement made with eyes open. To hold otherwise — that a warning from a distrusted hand warns nothing — would let every Warned Reader plead his carrier's bad name back into innocence, the same fraud T-451 refused for garble: the reader could always find a reason to distrust somebody and claim he never knew. The file judges notice by what reached the reader's eyes and what it said, never by whose hand carried it.

The second reason is that distrust cuts the other way with equal force, and the file must not pretend otherwise. A warning from a trusted hand that the reader ignores is still a warning he received; credit neither creates notice nor destroys it. And a warning the reader never read — because distrust made him discard it unread, because it arrived in a tongue he cannot read, because it never reached his desk — warns nothing, not because the carrier lacked credit but because the reader's eyes never met the sentence. The test is the Reader's Eyes: did the reader read a sentence naming echo-ness? If yes, he is a Warned Reader under T-450, whatever he thought of the carrier. If no, he is unwarned, whatever the carrier's standing. Delivery is not reading, and credit is not content.

The third reason is that separating notice from credit protects the file's own naming from becoming a popularity contest. If notice depended on carrier credit, the file would need a register of whom each reader trusts, and every placement would be graded on a reputation the file cannot verify — a second, shadow file of gossip standing beside the file of dates. T-450 already refused the carrier the power to discharge; T-452 refuses him the power to warn or un-warn by reputation either. The carrier's credit matters exactly once: to his own account. A distrusted carrier who carries faithfully has carried faithfully, and the reader he warned is warned. A distrusted carrier who garbles bears his garble under T-451, and the reader he misled is unwarned. In neither case does the carrier's name change what the reader read — only what the reader read changes what the reader knows.

**T-453 — the Disbelieved Warning — designed:** T-452 left its disbelieved-warning problem named and open: whether a warning the reader reads but affirmatively disbelieves after investigation still counts as notice when he places — whether investigation that concludes the warning false restores innocence, or whether only the file's naming can clear a doubt a carrier raised. T-453 answers: the doubt sticks until the file clears it. A reader who reads the warning, investigates, and concludes it false places as a Contested Reliance, not an innocent one: he places knowing a doubt was raised against his leg, and his private conclusion does not erase the notice, because notice is a fact about what reached his eyes under T-452's Reader's Eyes test, and a private investigation is not a fact in the file. Only the file's own naming — echo, date, and third mark together — or a third mark meeting T-444's threshold can clear the doubt. Until then the reader places at his own risk: if the file later confirms the echo, he cannot plead innocence, and if the file clears the leg, his date stands without re-filing.

The first reason is that a private investigation is unverifiable in the file, and clearance must be an act the file can check. The file can verify its own naming: a reader who meets it there can check the echo, the date, and the third mark together. It cannot verify the reader's private inquiry — what he checked, how far he went, whether his sources were independent of the carrier or downstream of the echo itself. To let private investigation clear a public warning would let every Warned Reader manufacture innocence in his own study and present it as fact, and the file would have to take his word for the clearance exactly where the whole echo danger is that a word can travel without its file. Notice is cleared by an act the file can check, never by an act only the reader witnessed.

The second reason is that disbelief is not clearance, and the asymmetry is the whole point. A reader who disbelieves after investigation faces two live possibilities: his investigation was right, and the leg is not an echo, or his investigation was wrong, and his sources were the echo's own downstream wearing the shape of confirmation. He cannot tell which from inside his investigation, because the echo's danger is precisely that it looks like a second seeing. Placing on a disbelieved warning is therefore a gamble the reader takes knowingly, and the file files the gamble, not the innocence. If his investigation was right and the file later clears the leg, the gamble pays and no correction is owed. If it was wrong, the Echo Correction reaches him as a Warned Reader, not as an innocent one: the correction still names the third mark his date actually stands on, but his posture is Contested Reliance, and he cannot claim the file failed to warn him, because the file's warning reached his eyes and his own investigation answered it in private.

The third reason is that the rule keeps the warning challengeable without making it erasable by fiat. The warning is not a verdict — T-450 already refused it discharge power, and T-453 refuses it the opposite power too: it does not become unchallengeable merely because it was carried. The reader may challenge it, but the challenge runs through the file: he brings his investigation to the file, the file checks it against the third mark, and the file's naming settles it. A doubt raised in public is answered in public. A reader who keeps his challenge private keeps his doubt too — and a reader who teaches his private clearance downstream teaches a clearance the file never gave, which files as his act, never as the file's.

**T-454 — the Pending Challenge — designed:** T-453 left its pending-challenge problem named and open: whether a reader's investigation brought to the file but not yet ruled on suspends the Echo Correction or merely queues it, and whether the reader who places while his challenge is pending places as contested or as suspended. T-454 answers: the challenge queues the correction, it does not suspend it — and the reader who places while his challenge is pending places as a Contested Reliance bearing a Pending Challenge, not as a Suspended Reliance. The Echo Correction proceeds on its own schedule, naming the third mark the date actually stands on; the pending challenge does not hold it back, and the placement is not held in abeyance either, because a placement is an act the reader chose to make knowing a ruling was outstanding, and the file files acts, not waits.

The first reason is that suspension would hand every challenger a veto by filing. If bringing a challenge to the file froze the Echo Correction until the file ruled, any reader who wanted his warned date left alone could freeze it indefinitely by lodging a challenge and letting it sit unruled — the correction that T-448 made one-per-placement, direct, and naming would become optional for anyone willing to file paper. A queue preserves the file's motion: the correction arrives, the challenge is heard, and the ruling still has full effect when it lands. If the file clears the leg, the correction is withdrawn and the date stands without re-filing, exactly as T-453 promised for a cleared leg. If the file confirms the echo, the correction stands, and the challenge does not die with the old placement — it survives against the corrected leg, because the challenger disputed the warning, not the date, and the corrected leg is the leg he must now answer.

The second reason is that a placement while pending is a gamble taken with eyes open, and the file must file the gamble, not the wait. A Suspended Reliance would pretend the reader placed nothing until the ruling, and would let him keep the benefit of the date while disowning the act of placing it — the same private-clearance trick T-453 refused, wearing a procedural mask. Contested Reliance with a Pending Challenge flag preserves both facts at once: he placed, and his challenge was live when he placed. If the ruling later clears the leg, the flag lifts and the date stands clean, and no correction is owed. If the ruling confirms the echo, the Echo Correction finds him as a Contested Reliance, not as an innocent one and not as a reader who was waiting — he cannot plead that he placed before the file spoke, because the file had already warned him, his own challenge proves he knew the warning was live, and his placement was made under that knowledge.

The third reason is that only a filed pending counts, and the distinction is what keeps the queue honest. A challenge is pending when it is brought to the file — dated, showing the investigation the reader relies on, and lodged where the file can rule on it against the third mark. A challenge merely announced downstream, told to other readers, or kept in the reader's study is not pending at all: it is T-453's private investigation in another coat, and it buys neither a queue entry nor a flag. The file cannot queue what was never lodged with it, and a reader who teaches his pending challenge downstream teaches a posture the file never gave, which files as his act, never as the file's. Filed pending earns the queue and the flag; announced pending earns nothing, and the correction proceeds as if it had never been spoken.

**T-455 — the Challenge Deadline — designed:** T-454 left its challenge-deadline problem named and open: how long a challenge may sit unruled before it lapses or is deemed abandoned — whether the file owes a ruling deadline, or whether a challenger who lets his challenge age has abandoned it by inaction. T-455 answers: the file owes the deadline, and the deadline is a term of the queue, not a judgment on the challenge — a challenge unruled when its term expires lapses, and a lapsed challenge loses its queue entry and its Pending Challenge flag, but decides nothing about the leg; and a challenger whose challenge lapsed through the file's own delay may re-file on the same investigation, while a challenger who abandoned his challenge may re-file only on new investigation.

The first reason is that a queue without a term is T-454's veto in slow motion. T-454 refused suspension because any reader could freeze the correction by filing and letting it sit; an open-ended queue hands the same reader the same freeze under a slower name — the correction proceeds, but the challenger keeps the flag, the posture of contest, and the threat of a ruling forever, and every later reader must place under a challenge that will never be answered. A term converts the queue from a wait into a tenancy: the challenge holds its place only for the term the file announced when the challenge was lodged, and when the term expires the place reverts. The term is announced at lodging and fixed there — a deadline moved after filing, or extended silently mid-queue, is not a term but a ruling disguised as procedure, and a file that moves its own deadline to kill a challenge it dislikes has ruled without meeting the third mark.

The second reason is that lapse is procedural, never substantive, and that is what keeps the deadline honest. A lapse neither confirms the echo nor clears the leg: the Echo Correction that already arrived stands on its own naming, and the placement keeps whatever posture the correction gave it — a Contested Reliance stays contested, a Warned Reader stays warned — minus only the Pending Challenge flag, which marked a live contest, not a standing one. A deadline that decided the leg would let the file rule by calendar, clearing or confirming without ever meeting the third mark; a deadline that merely ends the tenancy decides nothing, and the challenger who wants a ruling on the merits must earn it by re-filing, not inherit it from the clock. The flag lifts because the contest is no longer live; the placement does not change, because the placement was an act, and acts do not unhappen when a term expires. A ruling delivered after the term is void as a ruling on that challenge — it may still enter as the file's own fresh naming if it meets the Standing Correction form, but not as a ruling on a dead challenge, and whether such a naming binds readers who stood on the lapsed challenge is the stale-challenge problem, sharpened, not solved.

The third reason is that lapse and abandonment are different deaths, and the file must tell them apart, because they carry different re-filing rights. A challenge lapses when the file's own term expires with the challenge still standing and the challenger still answering — the delay is the file's, so the challenger keeps his investigation and may re-file on it; the file's slowness must not eat the challenger's standing. A challenge is abandoned when the challenger withdraws it, or when the file calls for the investigation papers and the challenger does not produce them, or when the challenger's own standing lapses — the death is the challenger's, so re-filing on the same investigation buys nothing; only new investigation earns a new queue entry, because the old one was not lost to the clock but surrendered. The distinction is the whole protection against both abuses at once: the file cannot kill a challenge by dawdling and then plead the deadline, and the challenger cannot kill his own challenge and then revive it unchanged.

**T-456 — the Extended Term — designed:** T-455 left its extension problem named and open: whether the file may extend its own term mid-queue — for instance when the third mark itself is under examination elsewhere — or whether any extension is a new term requiring re-lodging, and whether an extension announced to one challenger extends every pending challenge on the same leg. T-456 answers: the file may not extend a term by fiat mid-queue — an extension is a new term, and a new term requires re-lodging; but when the cause of the delay is the file's own examination, the re-lodging is the file's act, not the challenger's burden, and it preserves the original date; and an extension extends every pending challenge on the same leg only when its cause is leg-common, never when its cause is challenger-specific.

The first reason is that a term announced at lodging is a promise the file made to every reader, not only to the challenger, and a promise the file can quietly move is no promise at all. T-455 fixed the term at lodging precisely so that a file which dislikes a challenge cannot kill it by moving its own deadline — a deadline moved after filing is a ruling disguised as procedure. That protection dies the moment the file may extend by announcement alone: a file that can extend can also extend selectively, holding a favoured challenge alive while letting a disfavoured one lapse, and calling both acts procedure. A new term requiring re-lodging keeps the extension visible: the old term ends on its announced date, the new term begins on a new lodging date, and any reader can see the seam between them. The challenger who must re-lodge bears no penalty for the seam when the delay was the file's — the file re-lodges on his behalf, on his original investigation, with his original date preserved for priority — because the file's slowness must not eat the challenger's standing, the same rule T-455 set for lapse. The challenger who must re-lodge when the delay was his own — papers unproduced, standing lapsed — earns no preservation: his new term files as new, with a new date, because his old term died by his hand, not the file's.

The second reason is that the cause of the delay decides the scope of the extension, and the cause is either in the leg or in the challenger, never in both at once for the same delay. When the third mark itself is under examination elsewhere, the file cannot rule on any challenge against that leg — the ruling standard is the third mark, and a mark under examination cannot be met — so every pending challenge on that leg is delayed by the same cause, and an extension for one is an extension for all, announced once, to the leg, not to the challenger. When the delay is challenger-specific — one challenger's papers outstanding, one challenger's standing in question — the cause touches only that challenger, and an extension announced to him extends nobody else; other challengers on the same leg keep their own terms, lapse on their own dates, and are not held hostage to a stranger's slow papers. A file that extends one challenger's term and lets the extension travel silently to the whole leg has granted every other challenger a tenancy none of them asked for and none of them can be charged with; a file that withholds a leg-common extension from one challenger while granting it to another has ruled against that challenger without meeting the third mark.

The third reason is that a re-lodging the file performs must still be confirmed by the challenger, because a tenancy held for a reader who no longer stands is a tenancy held against the file. The file's automatic re-lodging preserves the date and the investigation, but it does not presume the challenger still stands: the challenger must confirm his standing within the new term's opening, or the re-lodged challenge lapses as abandoned, not as lapsed — the death is his, so re-filing on the same investigation buys nothing, by T-455's rule. This keeps the extension honest in both directions: the file cannot kill a challenge by dawdling, because its own delay triggers its own re-lodging; and a challenger cannot ride a file-caused extension forever, because his failure to confirm ends the tenancy by his own inaction, and the flag lifts with it. A confirmation that arrives after the new term's opening is a fresh filing, not a confirmation, and files as new.

**T-457 — the Late Confirmation — designed:** T-456 left its late-confirmation problem named and open: whether a challenger who confirms his standing late — after the new term's opening but before any ruling — may still be restored to the preserved date, or whether the late confirmation files as new and the preserved date is lost for good. T-457 answers: the late confirmation files as new, and the preserved date is not restored by the challenger's act — but the file may restore it by its own naming, and only while nothing has moved in reliance on the lapse. A late confirmation that arrives before any ruling on the leg, and before any reader has placed in reliance on the lapse, may be met by a Restoration Naming that restores the preserved date for priority; a late confirmation that arrives after a ruling, or after an intervening reliance, files as new and the preserved date is lost for good, not merely withheld.

The first reason is that the opening is a door, not a suggestion, and a door that stays open until the challenger chooses to walk through it is T-455's veto in slow motion. T-456 made confirmation within the new term's opening the act that keeps the file's re-lodging alive, precisely so that a challenger could not ride a file-caused extension forever. If a late confirmation restored the preserved date by the challenger's act alone, the opening would mean nothing: the challenger could confirm at any hour before a ruling and keep his date, and every later reader would place under a date that might spring back to life at any moment. Filing as new keeps the clock honest — the late confirmer stands from the date he actually confirmed, and no reader need guess whether a dead tenancy will revive.

The second reason is that restoration, when it happens, is the file's naming, not the challenger's right, and a naming harms no one only while nothing has moved. A ruling on the leg is a naming that settles standings; a placement made in reliance on the lapse is a reader building on ground the file left empty. To restore a preserved date after either would rewrite another reader's standing by grace — the late confirmer would leapfrog a reader who placed honestly, or stand ahead of a ruling that already spoke. But where neither has happened — no ruling, no intervening reliance — restoration rewrites nothing: the ground is still empty, the date still free, and the file's naming merely records that the challenger who still stands keeps the place he never truly abandoned. That is why restoration is possible at all, and why it is the file's act: only the file can see whether the ground moved, and only the file may name what its own queue still holds.

The third reason is that restoration restores the date for priority only, never the dead term. A restored challenger keeps his original date against readers who placed after the lapse, but his term runs from the restoration, not from the opening he missed — the new term he confirmed into is the term he lives under, and its announced end still binds him. To restore the term as well as the date would resurrect a tenancy that already died, and hand the late confirmer the very open-ended hold T-456 refused. And a challenger who confirms after a ruling, or after an intervening reliance, has not merely been late: his tenancy died and others built on its death, so restoration is impossible, not merely withheld — the file cannot unbuild what readers have built, and the late confirmer answers the ruling as it stands, from his new date.
